A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 26-year-old woman in a severe asthma exacerbation sits leaning forward with hunched shoulders and uses her accessory muscles. Loud wheezing earlier has faded, and now she has only decreased breath sounds with a prolonged expiration. What does the loss of wheezing most likely indicate?
opts: Her increased work of breathing, with accessory muscle use, leaning forward and hunched shoulders, argues against recovery. Tell: in a severe exacerbation, wheeze can vanish because too little air moves to make it.

Correct. Wheezing may not be present in severe exacerbations, which may show only decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration. With her accessory muscle use and posture, a quiet chest signals worse obstruction, not improvement.

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic in the differential, not an explanation for wheeze fading in a known severe exacerbation. Tell: decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration describe severe lower airway obstruction.
A good response would ease her work of breathing as the wheeze faded. Her accessory muscle use and posture persist. Tell: a quiet chest plus hard work of breathing means severe obstruction.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
A.q: A 34-year-old woman has had a cough for 10 days that began with a cold. Her sputum is green, and she asks for an antibiotic. Her temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation are normal, and her lungs have scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing and no focal findings. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Normal vital signs, no focal lung findings and rhonchi that clear with a cough describe uncomplicated acute bronchitis, usually a self-limited viral illness. Green or yellow sputum does not separate viral from bacterial infection, so no antibiotic is given; explain the expected course and agree on symptom goals.

Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin are not default bronchitis treatments, and antibiotic harms include adverse effects, Clostridioides difficile infection and resistance. Tell: a respiratory fluoroquinolone belongs to the community-acquired pneumonia pathway, not to a viral chest cold with normal vital signs.

Routine sputum culture and chest radiography are unnecessary in uncomplicated cases; imaging is for abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings or clinical risk that raise concern for pneumonia. She has none of these. Tell: order a test only when its result would change a decision.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is named as not a default bronchitis treatment, and routine antibiotics are not prescribed for uncomplicated bronchitis regardless of cough duration or sputum color. Her normal vital signs keep her out of the pneumonia pathway. Tell: green sputum alone never earns an antibiotic.

A.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
A.q: A 30-year-old man with asthma follows a written action plan. His personal best peak flow is 600 L/min. Today he is very short of breath, his quick-relief medicine has not helped, and his peak flow is 260 L/min. Which action-plan zone is he in?
opts: The yellow zone is 50% to 79% of personal best, 300 to 474 for him. At 260 he is below it, and quick-relief medicine has failed. Tell: failure of the quick-relief medicine is itself a red-zone criterion.

Waiting is unsafe: under 50% of personal best with failed quick-relief medicine is the red, medical-alert zone, which calls for action now. Tell: action plans are built so that a red reading leads to immediate action, not a delay.

Correct. A peak flow of 260 out of a personal best of 600 is about 43%, below 50% of personal best, and he is very short of breath despite quick-relief medicine. Those are red-zone, medical-alert findings: take the rescue medicine and call the doctor or get help now.
Green requires 80% or more of personal best (480 or higher) and no symptoms. He is far below that and very short of breath. Tell: he has none of the doing-well features.

B.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
B.q: In a patient with a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70, a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 42% predicted corresponds to which airflow grade?
opts: Grade 1, mild, requires 80% predicted or more. At 42% this patient is far below it. Tell: grade 1 is the only grade with near-normal airflow. Mild airflow limitation means near-normal airflow.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted. At 42% this patient is below the 50% line. Tell: under 50% moves the grade to severe. Grade 2 covers 50% to 79% predicted only.
Correct. Grade 3, severe, covers a post-bronchodilator 1-second volume of 30% up to 50% predicted, so 42% falls there. Grade 2 starts at 50% and grade 4 is below 30%.
Grade 4, very severe, is below 30% predicted. At 42% this patient is above that line. Tell: 30% to 49% is grade 3. Very severe means less than a third of predicted airflow.

B.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
B.q: Which spirometry pattern before a bronchodilator signals airflow limitation in asthma?
opts: Correct. Before a bronchodilator, airflow limitation shows as a reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second and a reduced ratio of that volume to forced vital capacity. Improvement after the bronchodilator then supports asthma.

A normal ratio with a low forced vital capacity suggests restriction, a filling problem. Asthma's obstruction lowers both the 1-second volume and the ratio. Tell: in obstruction the 1-second volume falls more than the vital capacity, so the ratio drops.

Obstruction lowers, not raises, the forced expiratory volume in 1 second, and the ratio to forced vital capacity falls too. Tell: air leaves the narrowed airway slowly, so less of it gets out in the first second.

Values improve after a bronchodilator in asthma rather than fall, and before it the 1-second volume and the ratio are reduced. Tell: a positive response is a rise of 12% or more in the 1-second volume, not a drop.

B.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
B.q: A 69-year-old woman on home oxygen has dry, cracked lips and uses a petroleum jelly lip balm several times a day. Which teaching applies?
opts: Switch her oxygen to a non-rebreather

A non-rebreather mask is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. Dry lips are not an indication to switch, and the mask would not address the balm. Tell: her issue is a product, not the delivery device.

Correct. Petroleum-based products such as lip balms, lotions, oils and grease are to be avoided with home oxygen. Her petroleum jelly lip balm, used several times a day, is exactly that, so she should stop it. Her dry lips are not a reason to keep using it.
Use more balm to protect the lips

Using more balm adds more of what home oxygen teaching says to avoid: petroleum-based lip balms, lotions, oils and grease. Dry lips do not change that. Tell: protecting the lips with a petroleum product conflicts with oxygen safety.

Stopping her oxygen is not called for. The teaching is to avoid petroleum-based products while keeping oxygen use safe, not to discontinue oxygen. Tell: remove the hazard, which is the balm, and keep the oxygen.

B.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 67-year-old man has a myocardial infarction and is placed on oxygen in the ambulance although his saturation was 98%. Which effect of oxygen makes this a problem?
opts: Correct. His saturation was 98%, so he was not hypoxic. Oxygen is not given in a myocardial infarction unless the saturation is below 91%, because oxygen causes vasoconstriction. Giving it to a man with a normal saturation exposes him to that effect without benefit.

Carbon dioxide retention is a listed hazard of oxygen, but it is not the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction; that reason is vasoconstriction. Tell: the myocardial infarction rule points to vasoconstriction.

Mucosal irritation is the dryness and soreness of the nose from oxygen, especially without humidity at higher flows. It does not explain why oxygen is avoided in a myocardial infarction. Tell: irritation is local; vasoconstriction is the cardiac concern.

Fire risk is real around any oxygen, but it does not explain why oxygen is withheld at a saturation of 98% in a myocardial infarction. Tell: the myocardial infarction caution is about vasoconstriction, not ignition.

B.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
B.q: A 20-year-old man has daily asthma symptoms and uses albuterol daily, but he wakes at night only once a month and has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 85% predicted. He has some limitation playing pickup basketball. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Mild persistent asthma allows symptoms and rescue use on more than 2 days a week but not daily. His are daily. Tell: the word daily is the line between mild and moderate persistent asthma.

Correct. Daily symptoms, daily short-acting beta-2 agonist use and some limitation of activity are moderate persistent features. Even though his night waking and 85% function are milder, severity is assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs.

His night waking and lung function look intermittent, but daily symptoms and daily rescue use far exceed the intermittent limit of 2 or fewer days a week. Tell: severity follows the worst feature, not the best ones.

Severe persistent asthma requires symptoms throughout the day, rescue use several times a day, extreme limitation or function below 60%. He uses albuterol daily with some limitation and 85% function. Tell: daily rescue use is moderate; several times a day is severe.

B.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
B.q: A 44-year-old man who drank methanol has a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L) and a carbon dioxide of 29 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). By the Winter formula, what does his carbon dioxide show?
opts: An added respiratory acidosis is shown by a carbon dioxide higher than the Winter prediction, above 31 here. His 29 is inside the range of 27 to 31. Tell: compute 1.5 x 14 + 8 before calling it a second disorder.

A respiratory alkalosis is a primary fall in carbon dioxide, and his fall is fully accounted for by the compensation the Winter formula predicts, 27 to 31. No second disorder is needed to explain a 29. Tell: inside the range means compensation alone explains it.
ruled out by a stated finding

Impending respiratory failure is signaled when the carbon dioxide is higher than the Winter prediction, with an added respiratory acidosis. His 29 is within the expected 27 to 31. Tell: the warning is a carbon dioxide above the range.

Correct. Winter formula: 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2, so 27 to 31. His 29 sits inside that range, so the fall in carbon dioxide is the expected respiratory compensation for his elevated-gap metabolic acidosis from methanol, with no second disorder.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 55, 58, 59

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 9-year-old boy has influenza with a temperature of 102.8°F and body aches. His parent wants to give him a fever medicine from the cabinet at home. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Acetaminophen is one of the listed antipyretics for influenza supportive care and is appropriate for a child. Tell: the antipyretic to avoid under 18 is aspirin, because of its association with Reye syndrome.

Ibuprofen is one of the listed antipyretics for influenza supportive care. Tell: the age warning applies to aspirin, which is avoided in anyone younger than 18 with influenza because of Reye syndrome.

Correct. Aspirin is avoided in children younger than 18 years with influenza because it is associated with Reye syndrome. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen is used for fever as part of supportive care, along with rest and fluids.
Rest and hydration are the core of influenza supportive care, especially when fever and poor intake cause mild volume depletion. Tell: the measure to avoid is a drug, aspirin, not fluids.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 74-year-old man has 3 days of fever to 102.6°F, shaking chills, a cough with purulent sputum and a stabbing right-sided chest pain on breathing. His respiratory rate is 28/min. Over the right lower lobe there are crackles and dullness to percussion. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. High fever, chills, purulent productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and tachypnea are more severe than a cold or bronchitis, and the findings sit over one lobe: crackles and dullness to percussion. Acquired outside the hospital, this is community-acquired pneumonia.

Aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile chemical injury with abrupt respiratory decline after a witnessed aspiration. Nothing in his story describes an aspiration event. Tell: pneumonitis follows abruptly after a witnessed aspiration; his illness is an infectious syndrome over days.

Acute bronchitis may cause a low-grade fever and cough, but consolidation should not be detected; if it is, think pneumonia. His crackles and dullness over one lobe are consolidation. Tell: bronchitis wheeze is central over the bronchial airways, not a focal lobar finding.
ruled out by a stated finding

A lung abscess is usually insidious and prolonged, over weeks, with foul-smelling sputum and sometimes hemoptysis, and imaging shows a cavity with an air-fluid level. His illness is 3 days old with lobar consolidation signs. Tell: abscess is slow and foul; this is acute and lobar.

B.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
B.q: Using about 2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg acutely and 5 per 10 chronically, which bicarbonate fits acute respiratory alkalosis with a carbon dioxide of 30 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44, midpoint 40) from a baseline bicarbonate of 24?
opts: 19 is 24 - 5, which applies the chronic response of 5 per 10 mm Hg. The stem is acute, where the fall is 2 per 10: 24 - 2 = 22. Tell: acute uses 2, chronic uses 5.
Correct. The carbon dioxide fell 10 mm Hg (40 to 30), and acute respiratory alkalosis lowers bicarbonate about 2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg. So 24 - 2 = 22 mEq/L is the expected bicarbonate.
24 assumes no compensation at all. Even acutely, bicarbonate falls about 2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg of carbon dioxide decline: 24 - 2 = 22. Tell: alkalosis lowers bicarbonate from baseline.
ruled out by a stated finding
26 is a rise in bicarbonate, the direction seen with respiratory acidosis. Alkalosis lowers it: 24 - 2 = 22. Tell: for a low carbon dioxide, bicarbonate falls.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 59

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 42-year-old poultry farmer has fever, a nonproductive cough, severe headache and a unilateral lower-lobe infiltrate. Psittacosis is suspected. Which test is most useful for timely confirmation?
opts: Correct. A respiratory nucleic acid amplification test, such as polymerase chain reaction, is timely and sensitive for Chlamydia psittaci, coordinated with public health laboratories. His poultry exposure and the lower-lobe infiltrate make that the confirming test.
The complete blood count and liver enzymes assess how ill the patient is, not the cause. They cannot identify Chlamydia psittaci. Tell: severity tests and organism tests answer different questions.

Serology often requires paired samples and can cross-react with other Chlamydia species, so one titer is neither timely nor specific. Tell: for a quick, sensitive answer, test respiratory secretions with a nucleic acid test.

Routine bacterial culture does not detect Chlamydia psittaci, an obligate intracellular bacterium. Tell: a culture will come back negative even when psittacosis is present, so it cannot confirm the suspicion.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 68-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 45% predicted, a 6-minute walk distance of 200 meters, a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 3, and a body mass index of 20. What is his BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index score?
opts: Five undercounts by 2, as if the walk distance were scored 0 or the dyspnea grade missed. Tell: 200 meters scores 2 and a dyspnea grade of 3 scores 2.
Six misses 1 point, most often the body mass index: a value of 21 or less scores 1. Tell: his body mass index of 20 adds the final point to reach 7. A total of 7 predicts about 18% 4-year survival.

Correct. 1-second volume 45% (36 to 49) = 2 + walk 200 meters (150 to 249) = 2 + dyspnea grade 3 = 2 + body mass index 20 (21 or less) = 1, for a total of 7. A score of 7 to 10 predicts about 18% 4-year survival.
Eight overcounts by 1, as if the 1-second volume of 45% scored 3. Tell: 3 points is for 35% or less; 36% to 49% scores 2. His total stays at 7. Recount: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1.

B.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
B.q: A 70-year-old man with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 6 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1. He had 2 moderate exacerbations treated at home in the past year. Under the current three-group scheme, which group is he in?
opts: Few symptoms with high risk would be C in the 2020 four-group scheme. Tell: in the current scheme C and D merged into E, so 2 moderate exacerbations make him E whatever his symptoms.
Group B is low risk with more symptoms; he has few symptoms and high risk. Tell: 2 moderate exacerbations put him in E. B also requires more symptoms, and his score is 6.

Correct. Two moderate exacerbations in the past year make him high risk, and any high-risk patient is group E regardless of symptoms. His low symptom score of 6 does not change that; group E starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic.
His symptoms (score 6, dyspnea grade 1) would fit group A, but 2 moderate exacerbations make him high risk. Tell: exacerbation risk overrides symptoms in the current scheme.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 47-year-old man tore down an old barn where bats roosted. Six days later he has high fever, chills, myalgias and a nonproductive cough. An early urine Histoplasma antigen is negative, but suspicion remains high. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Amphotericin-based induction is for severe pulmonary or disseminated disease, and he has a mild acute illness that is not yet confirmed. Tell: the open question is the diagnosis, which repeat testing answers.

Cryptococcus is inhaled from the environment and is a risk mainly with immunocompromise, and nothing in his story points to it. Tell: bat droppings point to Histoplasma, so the next move is to retest for Histoplasma.

Correct. Early negative tests do not exclude histoplasmosis. When suspicion persists, testing is repeated or respiratory specimens are obtained. His bat exposure and typical illness keep suspicion high, so one early negative result does not end the workup.

An early negative antigen test does not exclude disease; the antigen may not yet be detectable. Tell: a negative result early in the illness, with a strong exposure history, calls for repeat testing or respiratory specimens.

B.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 64-year-old man with pneumonia has an arterial blood gas before and after starting oxygen. After oxygen, his arterial oxygen pressure is higher, his carbon dioxide is unchanged, and his pH has returned toward normal. How is this response read?
opts: A saturation of 100% is not required. The saturation is judged against a target that varies with the patient, and his gas already shows a good response. Tell: the target varies, so 100% is not the goal.

Carbon dioxide retention would show a rising arterial carbon dioxide. His carbon dioxide is unchanged, so there is no sign of retention. Tell: unchanged carbon dioxide is what a good response requires.
ruled out by a stated finding

His arterial oxygen pressure rose and his pH corrected, which are the objective signs of response. There is a response. Tell: rising oxygen pressure with correcting pH is the pattern of a good response.

Correct. A good response is an increase in arterial oxygen pressure without an increase in arterial carbon dioxide, plus correction of the pH. His oxygen pressure rose, his carbon dioxide stayed unchanged, and his pH moved back toward normal, which meets all three.

B.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
B.q: A 50-year-old woman with a metabolic alkalosis from repeated vomiting has generalized weakness and hyporeflexia. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.52 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 48 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 38 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which laboratory finding best explains her weakness and hyporeflexia?
opts: Her mildly raised carbon dioxide of 48 is compensation for the alkalosis; severe hypercapnia causes somnolence and confusion, not hyporeflexia. Tell: the weakness of metabolic alkalosis comes from potassium.
Hyperkalemia accompanies acidosis, as potassium shifts out of cells. Her pH is 7.52, and alkalosis shifts potassium into cells. Tell: alkalosis means low potassium.
Correct. Metabolic alkalosis brings hypokalemia (potassium shifts into cells, and vomiting adds losses), and the associated hypokalemia causes weakness and hyporeflexia. Her alkalemia at 7.52 fits.
Her bicarbonate is 38, high, which is what defines her metabolic alkalosis. A low bicarbonate belongs to metabolic acidosis. Tell: read her bicarbonate before choosing.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
B.q: An 84-year-old woman has mild breathlessness she attributes to deconditioning. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of 0.68 with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 85% predicted. Which consideration applies before labeling her with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: In older adults the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose. Tell: her age and borderline value call for clinical context, not an automatic label.
Triple therapy is considered for high-risk group E patients with eosinophils of 300 or more. Tell: she has not even been confirmed, and her symptoms are mild.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing is aimed at young patients or those with few exposures, and mild breathlessness at 84 with a borderline ratio does not point to it. Tell: in an elderly patient the stated caution is overdiagnosis from the fixed ratio.

Correct. In adults 65 and older, the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose, so clinical context is weighed. A borderline ratio with near-normal airflow and mild symptoms in an 84-year-old calls for that judgment.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a resting oxygen saturation of 85% on room air on 2 visits, with no cor pulmonale (right heart failure). Which treatment is indicated?
opts: Evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea is the step when desaturation happens at night only. Tell: his desaturation is at rest while awake, which calls for long-term oxygen.
Long-term oxygen for over 15 hours a day

Correct. Severe resting desaturation, a saturation of 88% or less at rest, qualifies for long-term oxygen therapy for more than 15 hours a day. Oxygen for severe resting hypoxemia decreases the risk of death, prolongs life and improves quality of life.
No oxygen until saturation falls below 80%
The threshold is a resting saturation of 88% or less (or an arterial oxygen pressure under 55 mmHg), not 80%. Tell: 85% at rest already qualifies, and waiting forfeits a survival benefit.
Exertion-only oxygen is for patients who desaturate to 88% or less with exertion but not at rest. Tell: his saturation is 85% at rest, which qualifies him for oxygen most of the day.

B.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
B.q: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy has a routine arterial blood gas for mild breathlessness: pH 7.46 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Respiratory acidosis is a high carbon dioxide with a low pH. She has a low carbon dioxide of 28 and a high pH of 7.46. Tell: both values point the opposite way.

Correct. The pH of 7.46 is alkalemia, and the carbon dioxide of 28 is low and matches it: respiratory alkalosis. Bicarbonate fell about 5 per 10 mm Hg (12 below 40 gives about 18 to 19), a chronic renal response. Pregnancy is a listed endocrine cause.

Her bicarbonate is low, but her pH of 7.46 is high, so this is not an acidosis. The low bicarbonate is compensation for the respiratory alkalosis. Tell: the pH direction identifies the primary disorder.

Acute compensation lowers bicarbonate only about 2 per 10 mm Hg, to about 22 (12 below 40). Her 19 shows the fuller chronic response. Tell: pregnancy is a sustained state, so the kidneys have had time.

B.q: What risk of death does a CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) total of 2 carry?
opts: A risk of death under 3% belongs to a total of 0 to 1, low severity, usually treated at home unless there are other reasons for admission. Tell: 2 points is moderate severity, about 9%.

Correct. A total of 2 points is moderate severity, with a risk of death of about 9%, and the pathway sends these patients to the hospital. A total of 0 to 1 is low severity (under 3%), and 3 to 5 is high severity (15 to 40%).
A 15 to 40% risk belongs to a total of 3 to 5, high severity, with urgent senior review and consideration of critical care. Tell: 2 points is moderate, about 9%.
About 27% is the mortality of Pneumonia Severity Index class V, a different score. Tell: the five-item score at 2 points carries about 9%.

B.q: What is the primary risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic risk found even in nonsmokers, but it is rare, about 3 or 4 cases per 10,000. Tell: it is evaluated in young or unexposed patients, while tobacco remains the primary cause.
Burning wood or coal indoors for cooking and heating is a secondary risk factor, larger in developing countries. Tell: worldwide, the primary risk factor is tobacco smoking or exposure.

A sedentary lifestyle with limited activity is listed among risk factors, but it is not the primary one. Tell: the dominant risk is inhaled tobacco smoke, which is why smoking cessation can slow progression.

Correct. Tobacco smoking or exposure is the primary risk factor, behind about 90% of cases. Secondary risks are biomass burning, occupational dusts and fumes, a sedentary lifestyle and, much more rarely, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: Why can a mycobacterial culture take weeks to return a result?
opts: Smear conversion is not a precondition for reading a culture; the smear and the culture are requested together on each specimen. Tell: the delay belongs to the slow-growing organism, not to any other test.
The three sputum specimens are collected 8 to 24 hours apart and each is sent for smear and culture; they are not pooled. Tell: the weeks come from slow growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Molecular tests run alongside the culture, not before it, and they are the fast part of the workup. The culture is slow because of the organism. Tell: molecular tests are the rapid result, culture is the slow one.

Correct. Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, so cultures can take weeks. That is why a rapid molecular test is run on at least one respiratory specimen alongside the smear and culture: molecular tests can give results quickly.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
B.q: A 19-year-old college student has had episodes of wheezing, chest tightness and cough for 2 years, worse at night and after cleaning his dusty dorm room. He has allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Between episodes his lung exam is normal. Spirometry shows a reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second that improves 18% after albuterol. Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Intrinsic asthma is non-atopic and of later, adult onset, often with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity. This 19-year-old has rhinitis, eczema and a dust trigger, an atopic picture. Tell: the atopic triad and an allergen trigger point to extrinsic, not intrinsic, asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic in the differential, but it would not produce reversible lower airway obstruction on spirometry or travel with eczema and rhinitis. Tell: reversible obstruction plus atopy places the problem in the lower airways, not the larynx.

Correct. Episodic wheeze, chest tightness and cough worse at night, a dust trigger, allergic rhinitis and eczema (the atopic triad), a normal exam between episodes, and an 18% rise in the 1-second volume after albuterol (12% or more is a positive response) make allergic, extrinsic asthma the diagnosis.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a lower airway mimic, but its obstruction is largely irreversible and it follows years of smoke exposure. This student's obstruction reversed by 18% after albuterol. Tell: a large bronchodilator response in a young atopic patient supports asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 77-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and osteoporosis takes triple inhaled therapy. She has had 2 pneumonias this year and a wrist fracture after a fall. Which component of her regimen is linked to both pneumonia and fracture risk?
opts: Correct. Inhaled corticosteroids increase the risk of pneumonia, and in older adults the concerns include inhaled corticosteroid-related pneumonia and fracture risk. Her repeated pneumonias and fracture make that component the one to reassess.

Long-acting beta agonists carry cardiac risk, such as tachycardia, arrhythmias and worsening atrial fibrillation, not pneumonia or fractures. Tell: pneumonia and fracture together point to the steroid component.
Long-acting antimuscarinics are poorly absorbed, with mainly dry mouth. Tell: in older adults the drug tied to pneumonia and fractures is the inhaled corticosteroid.
Excessive albuterol risks cardiac and psychiatric side effects, not pneumonia or fractures. Tell: her 2 pneumonias and fracture fit the inhaled corticosteroid's risks.

B.q: A 46-year-old woman with nonsevere community-acquired pneumonia treated as an outpatient is afebrile, eating and clinically stable on day 3. What is the shortest total antibiotic course that may be appropriate for her?
opts: Correct. For clinically stable, nonsevere community-acquired pneumonia, a course shorter than 5 days, with a minimum of 3 days, may be appropriate. She is stable by day 3. Severe pneumonia is different: at least 5 days and until clinical stability.

Five days is the minimum for severe community-acquired pneumonia, which is treated for at least 5 days and until clinical stability. She has nonsevere disease and is stable. Tell: nonsevere and stable may stop sooner, with 3 days as the floor.

Seven days is the usual course for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia when the response is adequate. She has outpatient community-acquired pneumonia. Tell: 7 days belongs to the hospital pathway, not to a stable outpatient.

Ten days goes beyond what the current update requires for her. Long courses are for complications or specific pathogens, while a stable nonsevere pneumonia may stop after as few as 3 days. Tell: the update shortened courses for stable patients.

B.q: A 55-year-old woman with known hypercalcemia has a metabolic alkalosis, a high urine chloride and a normal blood pressure. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 45 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). In which group of metabolic alkalosis does she belong?
opts: Saline-responsive alkalosis has a low urine chloride (below 25 mEq/L) and volume contraction. Hers is high. Tell: high urine chloride rules out the responsive type.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A high urine chloride (above 40 mEq/L) marks saline-unresponsive alkalosis; with a normal blood pressure it is the normotensive group, which lists hypoparathyroidism and hypercalcemia and severe potassium depletion.

The hypertensive group (primary aldosteronism, mineralocorticoids, licorice) needs a raised blood pressure. Hers is normal, and hypercalcemia sits in the normotensive group. Tell: blood pressure splits the unresponsive causes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Post-hypercapnic alkalosis is saline responsive and follows rapid correction of chronic hypercapnia; she has neither a low urine chloride nor that history. Tell: it sits on the saline-responsive list.

B.q: A 48-year-old woman has coronavirus disease 2019 with fever, cough and mild shortness of breath. Her oxygen saturation is 96% on room air and her respiratory rate is 20/min, and a chest radiograph shows a patchy infiltrate. Which severity category fits?
opts: Mild illness has symptoms without shortness of breath and with a normal chest radiograph. Her radiograph shows an infiltrate and she is mildly short of breath. Tell: a positive radiograph is what separates moderate from mild.

Correct. Moderate illness has symptoms with a positive chest radiograph and an oxygen saturation of at least 94% on room air. Her patchy infiltrate makes her more than mild, and her saturation of 96% with a normal respiratory rate keeps her below severe.

Severe illness needs an oxygen saturation below 94% on room air, marked tachypnea or infiltrates over more than 50% of the lungs. Her saturation is 96% and her respiratory rate is 20. Tell: severe starts below 94%.
Critical illness means acute respiratory failure, septic shock or multiple organ dysfunction. She has none of these. Tell: a patchy infiltrate with normal oxygenation is moderate, far from critical.

B.q: A 52-year-old man has 12 mm of induration on a tuberculin skin test. His chest radiograph shows a fibrotic upper-lobe lesion, he does not recall ever being treated for tuberculosis, and he has no symptoms. Which step must come before latent-infection treatment?
opts: The blood test shows infection, which his skin test already shows, and neither test distinguishes latent infection from disease. Tell: the missing step is excluding active disease.
A repeat skin test in 8 to 10 weeks

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after exposure is for an early negative result after a recent exposure. Tell: his test is already positive, and his lesion raises the question of active disease, which must be excluded.
A second chest radiograph in 1 year

Waiting a year leaves possible active disease unaddressed; fibrotic lesions warrant exclusion of active disease now. Tell: imaging cannot reliably determine activity, so microbiology is needed before treatment.

Correct. Fibrotic lesions warrant review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease, and tuberculosis disease must be excluded before latent-infection treatment begins. Imaging cannot reliably determine activity, so microbiologic testing answers that question.

B.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure is hospitalized on day 5 of influenza, confirmed by molecular testing, with hypoxemia. Which antiviral is most appropriate?
opts: Amantadine and rimantadine are not recommended because of resistance. Tell: the hospital antiviral is oseltamivir, given orally or by enteric tube.

Inhaled zanamivir is avoided in chronic obstructive lung disease because of bronchospasm risk, and hospitalized patients generally receive oseltamivir instead. Tell: his lung disease and admission both rule out the inhaled drug.
ruled out by a stated finding
Baloxavir is not recommended for hospitalized influenza and is limited to uncomplicated illness within 48 hours. He is hospitalized on day 5. Tell: admission and timing both rule it out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Hospitalized patients generally receive oral or enteric oseltamivir, which is preferred for hospitalized, severe and high-risk patients and is started even after 48 hours. His age, lung and heart disease and admission all point to it, with renal dose adjustment.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman with severe community-acquired pneumonia in the intensive care unit had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from her sputum last year. She has been started on ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Which agent should be added?
opts: Moxifloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone that can partner a beta-lactam in severe pneumonia, but it is not a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus agent and is not reliable for Pseudomonas. Tell: the agents named for resistant staphylococcus are vancomycin or linezolid.

Clindamycin is held back even in lung abscess because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and it is not an agent listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia. Tell: the listed agents are vancomycin or linezolid.

Ertapenem is named as not a reliable antipseudomonal option and is not one of the agents listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: her validated risk is the resistant staphylococcus, so the add-on is vancomycin or linezolid.

Correct. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage is added only for validated risks, and a prior respiratory isolate is one. The agents named for it are vancomycin or linezolid, added to the beta-lactam combination; cultures are obtained and therapy de-escalated as results return.

B.q: On an arterial blood gas, an arterial oxygen pressure at or below what cutoff qualifies a patient for home oxygen with no comorbidity required?
opts: A cutoff of 50 mm Hg is lower than the stated 55 mm Hg and would exclude patients at 51 to 55 mm Hg, who qualify. The line with no comorbidity required is at or below 55 mm Hg. Tell: remember 55, not a round 50.

Correct. An arterial oxygen pressure at or below 55 mm Hg qualifies for home oxygen without any comorbidity (Group I). Readings of 56 to 59 mm Hg qualify only when pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or polycythemia is documented.

A value up to 59 mm Hg is not enough by itself. A pressure of 56 to 59 mm Hg is the conditional Group II range and needs pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or polycythemia as well. Tell: with no comorbidity, stop at 55 mm Hg.

A cutoff of 65 mm Hg is well above the qualifying range; the highest value that qualifies even with a comorbidity is 59 mm Hg. Tell: Group I is 55 mm Hg or lower, with 56 to 59 mm Hg needing a comorbidity.

B.q: A 35-year-old man with asthma and a body mass index of 36 asks how his weight relates to his asthma. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Obesity makes asthma harder to control

Correct. Asthma is more frequent in people with a body mass index above 30, and their symptoms are more difficult to control, although the mechanism is unknown. His body mass index of 36 places him in that group.
Obesity makes asthma symptoms more difficult to control, not milder. Tell: a body mass index above 30 is linked to more frequent asthma and harder control.
Obesity matters just for exercise-induced symptoms
The link between obesity and asthma is not limited to exercise; asthma is more frequent and harder to control overall above a body mass index of 30. Tell: the effect covers his asthma as a whole.
Obesity has no link to asthma
Obesity is a listed endogenous factor: asthma is more frequent in people with a body mass index above 30. Tell: weight is linked to both how often asthma occurs and how hard it is to control.

B.q: A 45-year-old woman with severe persistent asthma has needed 4 courses of oral corticosteroids this year despite confirmed adherence and good technique with her inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta-2 agonist. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Removing part of a regimen she uses correctly would not explain or fix her exacerbations. Tell: refractory, steroid-dependent asthma despite adherence calls for a specialist, who can offer agents that reduce the need for steroids.

Immunotherapy must be done in a controlled environment because it can induce bronchoconstriction, and it targets allergic triggers. Tell: her problem is refractory severe asthma, which calls for specialist care.
Refer to a lung or allergy specialist

Correct. With adherence and technique confirmed, her repeated steroid-requiring exacerbations make her asthma refractory. Monoclonal antibody agents are used by pulmonology and allergy specialists and reduced the need for corticosteroids in trials, so referral to a specialist fits.

Theophylline gives mild bronchodilation but has a narrow toxic-therapeutic range and is rarely used because of toxicity concerns. Tell: refractory disease needing repeated steroids is a specialist referral, where steroid-sparing antibody therapy is available.

B.q: A 66-year-old woman is expected to need mechanical ventilation for several days after a large stroke. Which measure helps prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?
opts: Proper positioning means elevating the head of the bed, the opposite of lying flat, because the pneumonia comes from colonized secretions inhaled through the tube. Tell: head up keeps secretions out of the lungs.
Elevating the head of the bed

Correct. Prevention is the main strategy for ventilator-associated pneumonia: early extubation, hand washing and sterile technique, limiting circuit changes, proper positioning with the head of the bed elevated, and supraglottic secretion drainage with mouth care.
Changing parts of the circuit is one of the ways contamination enters, so prevention limits circuit changes. Tell: fewer breaks in the circuit, not more, prevent this pneumonia.

Prior antibiotic use is listed among the contributors to ventilator pneumonia, and the prevention bundle relies on extubation, hygiene, positioning and secretion care. Tell: prevention here is mechanical and hygienic, not antibiotic.

B.q: A 29-year-old woman has had 9 days of coughing fits that end in vomiting, with a whooping sound on inspiration. Her nephew was diagnosed with pertussis last week. Her vital signs and lung examination are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Supportive care fits uncomplicated viral bronchitis, but suspected pertussis needs targeted testing and treatment to reduce spread to others. Her exposure and coughing fits make this more than a chest cold. Tell: transmission is the reason not to stop at reassurance.

Correct. Paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting, a whoop and a relevant exposure are the pertussis clues, and suspected pertussis needs targeted testing and treatment to reduce transmission. There is no need to wait for 4 weeks of cough before testing.

Imaging is obtained when vital signs, focal lung findings or clinical risk raise concern for pneumonia. Her vital signs and examination are normal. Tell: the pertussis clues call for organism-targeted testing, not a film of the lungs.

Waiting is the error the guidance warns against: do not wait for 4 weeks of cough when the pertussis clues are present. Her whoop, post-tussive vomiting and exposure already justify testing. Tell: the clues, not the length of the cough, trigger the workup.

B.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic is light-headed on standing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.49 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 46 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.2 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is low. Along with isotonic saline, which medication change is indicated?
opts: Mineralocorticoids cause a hypertensive, saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis, so adding one would worsen his. Tell: mineralocorticoids are on the cause list, not the treatment list.

Correct. Low urine chloride and orthostatic symptoms mark a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and diuretic therapy is a listed cause. Treatment is isotonic saline for the volume deficit and discontinuing the diuretic.
Antacids are a cause of saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, so starting one adds alkali to an alkalemia. Tell: antacid, diuretic and vomiting sit together on the cause list.
A second diuretic would deepen the volume contraction and the alkalosis; diuretics are discontinued in saline-responsive alkalosis. Tell: the drug causing the alkalosis is stopped, not doubled.

B.q: A 27-year-old man describes cough and chest tightness with cold air and smoke over several months. His spirometry is normal, with no meaningful change after albuterol. Asthma is still suspected. Which test is most appropriate next?
opts: The chest x-ray in asthma is usually normal or shows hyperinflation, so it adds little after normal spirometry. Tell: when spirometry fails to show asthma, the next step is to provoke airway hyper-responsiveness with methacholine.

Annual spirometry is for monitoring the progression of known disease, not for settling a suspected diagnosis today. Tell: when spirometry is not diagnostic, bronchial provocation testing is the next test.

Correct. Bronchial provocation testing with methacholine or histamine is useful when spirometry is not diagnostic, as here, where a typical history meets normal spirometry. His normal lung function also clears the rule that provocation is not done below 65% predicted.

An exercise challenge is the provocation test used when exercise-induced bronchospasm is suspected. His triggers are cold air and smoke, not exercise. Tell: for a nondiagnostic spirometry with general triggers, methacholine or histamine challenge is the test.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 47-year-old man moved 1 year ago from an area with high tuberculosis incidence. He has 6 weeks of productive cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss and hemoptysis, and his chest radiograph shows an upper-lobe cavity. His interferon-gamma release assay is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Nontuberculous disease is on the differential and causes chronic cough, weight loss and hemoptysis, with risk rising in bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and immune dysfunction. Tell: he has none of those, while his positive assay reflects tuberculosis-specific antigens.

Lung abscess is on the differential for fever, weight loss, hemoptysis and cavitary disease, because these findings have a broad differential. Tell: his origin in a high-incidence area and his positive interferon-gamma release assay make tuberculosis the leading cause, pending sputum testing.

Correct. Residence in a high-incidence area is an exposure risk, and persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss and hemoptysis are pulmonary manifestations; post-primary disease often involves the upper lobes and may cavitate. Imaging and the blood test support the suspicion; sputum microbiology confirms it.

Lung cancer is one of the other causes of cavitary disease on the differential. Tell: fever, night sweats, recent arrival from a high-incidence area and a positive interferon-gamma release assay point to tuberculosis, which microbiology then confirms.

B.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
B.q: What happens to carbon dioxide when ventilation increases?
opts: Correct. Increased ventilation decreases carbon dioxide, and decreased ventilation increases it. In the steady state, carbon dioxide production matches excretion, so changing ventilation shifts the balance.

Ventilation changes carbon dioxide directly; the steady state, with production matching excretion, holds only while ventilation stays constant. Increasing ventilation raises excretion, so carbon dioxide falls. Tell: when excretion exceeds production, the level cannot stay the same.

Carbon dioxide is not converted away here: increased ventilation removes carbon dioxide from the body, lowering it. Tell: ventilation clears carbon dioxide; the kidneys compensate for respiratory disorders by retaining or excreting bicarbonate.
Carbon dioxide rises with decreased ventilation, not increased. More ventilation blows it off, so it falls. Tell: more breaths mean more carbon dioxide leaves, fewer breaths mean it builds up.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 55-year-old woman with group B chronic obstructive pulmonary disease still smokes a pack a day. She asks what single step would do the most to slow her disease. Which intervention is most appropriate?
opts: Long-term azithromycin is not among the measures listed for improving survival. Tell: the intervention with a survival benefit is smoking cessation.

An inhaled corticosteroid adds pneumonia risk and must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist and raises pneumonia risk. Tell: no inhaler is the step that most helps survival; stopping smoking is.

Correct. Smoking cessation is the only treatment that can slow progression, and every attempt should be combined with counseling to increase efficacy; nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline can be added. It is essential for every group.
Chest computed tomography can categorize emphysema but is generally not needed, and imaging changes nothing about progression. Tell: her most powerful step is quitting smoking with counseling.

B.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
B.q: A 41-year-old man with asthma is reviewing his written action plan with you. Which finding is a danger sign telling him to take his quick-relief medicine and go to the hospital or call an ambulance now?
opts: Mild wheeze with the first signs of a cold
The first signs of a cold and mild wheeze are caution, or yellow-zone, features. Tell: those call for adding quick-relief medicine, while blue lips or fingernails call for the hospital now.

Night cough, like waking at night with asthma, is a yellow-zone sign that asthma is getting worse. Tell: yellow means add quick-relief medicine and keep the controller; the danger signs are blue lips or trouble walking and talking.
Peak flow at 75% of personal best

A reading of 75% of personal best falls in the yellow zone, 50% to 79%. Tell: the red zone starts below 50%, and the danger signs are blue lips or fingernails and trouble walking and talking from breathlessness.

Correct. The action plan's danger signs are trouble walking and talking because of shortness of breath, and lips or fingernails that are blue. Either one means take the quick-relief medicine and go to the hospital or call an ambulance now, without waiting.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 44-year-old man is about to start a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor. He has no symptoms of tuberculosis and has never been tested for it. Which step regarding tuberculosis is most appropriate before he starts?
opts: Sputum specimens are collected when pulmonary tuberculosis disease is suspected from symptoms or suspicious imaging. Tell: he is symptom-free, so the question is infection, answered by a skin test or interferon-gamma release assay.

Correct. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors raise the risk of progression after tuberculosis infection, and testing is targeted at people at increased risk. A skin test or interferon-gamma release assay detects the immune response to infection; a positive result then needs clinical evaluation and chest imaging.
No testing because he has no symptoms

Symptoms may be mild or absent, and testing targets people at increased risk, whether or not they have symptoms. Tell: his planned tumor necrosis factor inhibitor is a progression risk, which is the reason to test.
Latent-infection treatment follows a positive test and exclusion of disease. Tell: the first step is a test for infection; treatment decisions follow its result and a clinical evaluation.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 70-year-old woman with frequent exacerbations asks about taking azithromycin every day to prevent them, as a friend does. Which statement about long-term azithromycin is accurate?
opts: Long-term azithromycin is used rarely, not as routine first-line therapy. Tell: first-line maintenance is built from bronchodilators by group, with smoking cessation and rehabilitation.
No antibiotic replaces long-acting bronchodilators, which treat bronchoconstriction and prevent exacerbations. Tell: azithromycin would be an occasional add-on, not a substitute.
Long-term use increases side effects as well as resistance. Tell: the risks are why it is used rarely. Resistance can also limit future antibiotic choices.
It is rare and raises resistance

Correct. Some patients are put on long-term azithromycin or erythromycin, but this is rare, and it increases the risk of resistance and side effects. Frequent exacerbations despite optimal therapy are a reason for pulmonology referral.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
B.q: A 68-year-old woman taking theophylline for asthma has nausea, vomiting, headache and a rapid irregular heartbeat. Her potassium is low and her glucose high. Which explanation best fits her presentation?
opts: Correct. Theophylline has a narrow toxic-therapeutic range, and its toxic effects are nausea, vomiting, tachyarrhythmias, headache, seizure, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia, matching this woman's picture. That toxicity is why it is rarely used and needs close monitoring.

Inhaled corticosteroids cause local effects: hoarseness, cough and oral thrush. Their systemic side effects are minimal, so they do not explain vomiting, arrhythmia and low potassium. Tell: her systemic toxic picture belongs to the drug with a narrow toxic-therapeutic range, theophylline.

An aspirin-sensitive reaction brings rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, flushing and wheeze after aspirin, and aspirin is not part of her story. Tell: vomiting, arrhythmia, hypokalemia and hyperglycemia in a theophylline user point to toxicity.
ruled out by a stated finding

Muscle tremor and palpitations are the listed side effects of the short-acting beta-2 agonist class. Vomiting, headache and the arrhythmia with low potassium and high glucose are the listed toxic effects of theophylline, and the stem names theophylline. Tell: the whole cluster matches theophylline toxicity.

B.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes and an acute myocardial infarction has an oxygen saturation of 87% on room air. Which is the right approach to oxygen?
opts: Give oxygen, since saturation is below 91%

Correct. Her saturation of 87% is below the 91% cutoff. Oxygen is held back in a myocardial infarction because of vasoconstriction, but only while the saturation is 91% or higher. She is hypoxic, so the benefit of correcting hypoxia wins and she should receive oxygen.
Withhold oxygen because of her diabetes

Diabetes is not a listed reason to withhold oxygen. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction, and the myocardial infarction rule turns on a saturation under 91%. Tell: the saturation decides, not her comorbidity.
Wait for an arterial blood gas first

An arterial blood gas is not required before treating. A pulse oximeter reading of 87% already shows she is below 91%, and delaying oxygen leaves hypoxia uncorrected. Tell: the threshold rests on the saturation she already has; no extra test is needed to start.

Vasoconstriction is the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction, but that applies unless the saturation is below 91%. At 87% she is below it, so the exception applies. Tell: withhold when the saturation is 91% or higher, give when it is below 91%.

B.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
B.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
B.q: Sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), chloride 114 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106) and bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26). What is the calculated anion gap?
opts: Correct. Anion gap = 138 - (114 + 14) = 138 - 128 = 10, within the normal 9 to 15. With a low bicarbonate and a high chloride, this is a normal-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.
14 is the bicarbonate value itself, not the gap. The gap is calculated: 138 - (114 + 14) = 10. Tell: the gap comes from the subtraction, not a single listed value.
24 comes from 138 - 114, leaving out the bicarbonate. Subtract both measured anions: 138 - 128 = 10. Tell: the sum of chloride and bicarbonate is 128.
38 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (138 - 114 + 14). The gap is 138 - (114 + 14) = 10. Tell: add the two anions, then subtract the sum from sodium.

B.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
B.q: For an eligible adult who has never had a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, which vaccine type completes the series with one dose?
opts: The 15-valent conjugate vaccine does not finish the series alone: it is usually followed by the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine, typically at least 1 year later. Tell: the one-and-done options are the 20- and 21-valent vaccines.

The 23-valent vaccine is the polysaccharide vaccine, used after the 15-valent conjugate vaccine rather than as a single complete series. Tell: the single dose that completes the series is a 20- or 21-valent conjugate.
There is no 23-valent conjugate vaccine: the 23-valent product is the polysaccharide vaccine, and calling it a conjugate is a known error. Tell: the conjugate vaccines are 15-, 20- and 21-valent.

Correct. One dose of the 20-valent or 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine completes the series for a conjugate-naive eligible adult. The 15-valent conjugate vaccine, by contrast, usually needs the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine afterward.

B.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
B.q: A 24-year-old woman started an inhaled corticosteroid for moderate persistent asthma 1 week ago and wants to stop it because she does not feel much different yet. What should she be told?
opts: It is meant to be used during attacks

Inhaled corticosteroids are long-term controllers, not rescue medicines; attacks are treated with the short-acting rescue inhaler. Tell: a controller is taken every day and works gradually, over months.

Relief within minutes describes a short-acting beta-2 agonist, which relaxes smooth muscle and lasts about 3 to 6 hours. Tell: inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation slowly, with maximum response taking months.
Its full effect can take months

Correct. Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred first-line treatment for persistent asthma, and most patients respond to twice-daily dosing, but the maximum response may take months. One week is too early to judge, and stopping would leave her inflammation untreated.
Her lack of change means she needs oral steroids
Long-term systemic steroids are for refractory or poorly controlled cases, and 1 week cannot show failure of an inhaled steroid. Tell: maximum response to inhaled corticosteroids may take months.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
B.q: Which examination finding correlates with the degree of airway obstruction in asthma?
opts: Basilar inspiratory crackles suggest alveolar fluid or fibrosis, not asthma's airway obstruction. The finding that tracks obstruction is a prolonged expiratory phase. Tell: asthma's findings cluster on expiration, while crackles here are inspiratory.

Obstruction lengthens expiration rather than shortening it, because air leaves slowly through narrowed airways. A prolonged expiratory phase correlates with the obstruction. Tell: the more narrowed the airway, the longer it takes to breathe out.

Correct. A prolonged expiratory phase during normal respiration correlates with obstruction, because air takes longer to leave through narrowed airways. In severe exacerbations wheezing may disappear, leaving decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration.

A friction rub is a pericarditis sign and says nothing about airway obstruction. A prolonged expiratory phase correlates with obstruction in asthma. Tell: a rub is a heart sound tied to the cardiac cycle, not to breathing out.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 33-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus infection has never had Pneumocystis pneumonia. His CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count is 160 cells/mm³, and his viral load is detectable. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Primary prophylaxis starts for a CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count below 100 cells/mm³, or a count of 100 to 200 with a detectable viral load. His 160 with a detectable viral load meets the second criterion, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred drug.

Secondary prophylaxis follows a completed treatment course, but primary prophylaxis is meant to prevent the first episode in patients who meet the count criteria. Tell: he has never had the infection and already qualifies for primary prophylaxis.
Wait until the count is below 100

Below 100 is one trigger, but a count of 100 to 200 with a detectable viral load is the other, and he meets it. Tell: read both parts of the criterion; his detectable viral load brings the threshold up to 200.
No prophylaxis while he feels well

Prophylaxis is decided by the count and the viral load, not by symptoms; waiting for symptoms means waiting for the infection. Tell: a count of 160 with a detectable viral load qualifies him whether or not he feels well.

B.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
B.q: A 38-year-old woman develops an acute respiratory acidosis after aspiration pneumonitis two hours ago. When will her kidneys begin to compensate?
opts: In 6 to 12 hours, completing over days

Correct. In respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate; this begins 6 to 12 hours after onset, and complete compensation may take days. At two hours her bicarbonate is near normal.
Within minutes, completing in an hour
Breathing changes carbon dioxide quickly, but renal bicarbonate control works over hours to days. Tell: the kidneys are the slow system.
They do not; the lungs compensate instead
When the cause is respiratory, the compensation is renal: the kidneys retain or excrete bicarbonate. The lungs compensate for metabolic disorders. Tell: respiratory problem, renal fix.
Renal compensation begins within 6 to 12 hours and may be complete in days, not weeks. Tell: hours to start, days to finish.

B.q: A 17-year-old runner with exercise-induced bronchospasm uses albuterol before every practice, yet still has frequent symptoms during training. Which change is most likely to prevent his episodes?
opts: Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with a short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise but is best prevented with regular inhaled corticosteroid use. His frequent symptoms despite pre-exercise albuterol call for the regular controller.

Asthma treatment aims for no limitation on physical activity, so giving up running is not the goal. Tell: regular inhaled corticosteroid use best prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm and keeps him training.
Saving albuterol for after symptoms start

Albuterol helps most when used before exercise, and moving it to after symptoms begin gives up that protection. Tell: when pre-exercise albuterol is not enough, prevention comes from a regular inhaled corticosteroid.

Cromolyn prevents symptoms but does not relieve them once present, so taking it during an episode does not help. Tell: the agent that best prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm is a regular inhaled corticosteroid.

B.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 60-year-old man is found unresponsive and is not breathing. He has a pulse. A colleague reaches for a non-rebreather mask. Why does that device not fit his situation?
opts: Its fraction of oxygen is too low

A non-rebreather delivers a high fraction, 60-100% at 10-15 L/min, so a low fraction is not the problem. Its listed use is a severely hypoxic patient who is still ventilating well, and he is not breathing. Tell: the mask's strength is not in question; his breathing is.
ruled out by a stated finding
Its bag must collapse on each breath

The dosing rule is the reverse: prevent bag collapse on inspiration, at 10-15 L/min. A bag rule does not explain why the mask fails a man who is not breathing. Tell: the non-rebreather is for patients who are still ventilating well.
ruled out by a stated finding
It is a high flow oxygen device

The non-rebreather is a low flow device, but with a high fraction; the high flow device on the list is the Venturi mask. Its flow type is not what rules it out here. Tell: he fails the mask's requirement that the patient is still ventilating well.
ruled out by a stated finding
It is for patients ventilating well

Correct. He is unresponsive and not breathing, though he has a pulse. A non-rebreather mask is used in severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well, and he is not breathing at all, so the mask's listed use does not fit him.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 75-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a severe exacerbation. She is confused, her blood pressure is falling despite fluids, and she is tiring and may need invasive ventilation. Which level of care is most appropriate?
opts: More than 80% of exacerbations are managed outpatient, but only when the patient is stable. Tell: confusion and falling blood pressure place her at the other end, in intensive care.

Correct. Intensive care admission is for patients who are hemodynamically unstable, have a major infection or need invasive ventilatory support, and for sepsis, altered mental status, respiratory failure or respiratory acidosis. Her confusion, falling pressure and possible need for intubation meet these.

A ward fits admission criteria such as marked symptoms despite treatment or lack of home support. Tell: hemodynamic instability, altered mental status and possible invasive ventilation call for intensive care.
Rehabilitation is considered at discharge after an exacerbation, not during a critical one. Tell: her instability and tiring breathing call for intensive care.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 61-year-old man who smokes has coughed up thick sputum most days for 4 months of each of the last 3 years. He has rhonchi, bluish lips and swelling of both ankles. His blood gas shows low oxygen and raised carbon dioxide, and his diffusing capacity is near normal. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of 0.64. Which subtype best describes his disease?
opts: Emphysema brings a thin, pursed-lip breather with preserved gas exchange until late and a reduced diffusing capacity. He has early hypoxemia and hypercapnia with a near-normal diffusing capacity. Tell: sputum, cyanosis and edema point to bronchitis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not this disease, but his ratio of 0.64 confirms obstruction. Tell: once the ratio is below 0.70, his chronic cough places him in the chronic bronchitis subtype.
ruled out by a stated finding

Asthma does not usually bring years of daily sputum, cyanosis, edema and chronic carbon dioxide retention in a smoker. Tell: his cough history meets the chronic bronchitis definition, with persistent obstruction.

Correct. Productive cough for at least 3 months a year over 2 years, rhonchi, cyanosis, edema, early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and a near-normal diffusing capacity, with confirmed obstruction (ratio 0.64), are the chronic bronchitis picture (the blue bloater).

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 34-year-old woman who works in a setting with ongoing tuberculosis transmission has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on targeted testing. She has no symptoms, her examination is normal and her chest radiograph is normal. Which best describes her tuberculosis status?
opts: Correct. A positive interferon-gamma release assay shows infection, and her clinical evaluation found no evidence of disease: no symptoms, a normal examination and a normal radiograph, which is usual in latent infection. Latent infection is asymptomatic and not infectious.

Disease needs more than an immune response: symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss, or suspicious imaging, then microbiologic testing. Tell: she has none of these, and the blood test cannot by itself distinguish latent infection from disease.

Reactivation is latent infection that has progressed to disease, often with impaired immunity, so it brings symptoms or imaging findings. Tell: nothing here has progressed; she is still at the latent stage.

Progressive primary tuberculosis is disease that develops soon after initial infection when immune containment fails, so it brings clinical findings. Tell: a symptom-free woman with a normal examination and radiograph has contained infection, not progressive disease.
