C.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
C.q: A 37-year-old woman with asthma records her peak flow at home. Over the past week her morning readings before albuterol have been about 280 L/min and her afternoon readings after albuterol about 380 L/min. What does this pattern indicate?
opts: Good control would keep morning-to-afternoon variation under 20%. Her readings swing by about 36%. Tell: a large morning-to-afternoon gap is the hallmark of poor control, not good control.

Correct. Peak flow is measured in the morning before and the afternoon after the bronchodilator, and a 20% change between them, or day to day, indicates poor control. A rise from 280 to 380 is about 36% of the morning value (26% of the afternoon value), well over the 20% line.
Normal circadian variation needing no action

Bronchial reactivity does vary through the day, but a swing of more than 20% between morning and afternoon is defined as poor control and needs review. Tell: the 20% threshold separates expected variation from poor control.

A consistent pattern every morning and afternoon for a week, with higher readings after albuterol, fits real airway variation, not a broken device. Tell: the readings rise exactly when the bronchodilator works.

C.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
C.q: A 22-year-old college athlete with gastroenteritis has vomited for three days and is dizzy on standing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.51 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 48 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is low. In addition to treating the cause, which therapy is indicated?
opts: Diuretic therapy is a cause of saline-responsive alkalosis, and diuretics are stopped, not started, in this disorder. He needs volume, not more volume loss. Tell: discontinuing diuretics is part of the treatment.

Bicarbonate is alkali; exogenous alkali is itself a cause of metabolic alkalosis and would push his pH of 7.51 higher. Isotonic saline treats the volume loss behind his alkalosis. Tell: adding alkali to an alkalemia raises the pH further.

Breathing into a paper bag is not necessary even for hyperventilation: it fails to correct carbon dioxide and may decrease oxygen. His carbon dioxide is already raised as compensation. Tell: this is metabolic, and the fix is volume.

Correct. Vomiting (loss of hydrochloric acid) with orthostatic dizziness and a low urine chloride is saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, a sign of extracellular volume contraction. Isotonic saline corrects that volume deficit.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
C.q: At minimum, how often are adherence, symptoms and adverse effects reviewed during tuberculosis treatment?
opts: Weekly review is more often than required; the minimum is a review at least monthly, while directly observed therapy supports daily adherence. Tell: the minimum review interval is monthly.

Correct. Adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly, sputum cultures are followed until conversion, response is documented at 2 months, and liver injury, drug interactions and drug-specific toxicity are monitored.
Every 3 months is too infrequent; adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly. Tell: monthly, not quarterly.
Waiting until the end would miss liver injury, interactions and nonadherence along the way. Tell: the review happens at least monthly during treatment.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
C.q: A 25-year-old woman with asthma wakes most nights at about 3 in the morning with cough and wheeze, though she feels fine in the daytime. She asks why her symptoms come at night. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Bronchial reactivity peaks in the early morning hours

Correct. Asthma symptoms may be worse at night because of circadian variation in bronchomotor tone and bronchial reactivity, which peaks around 3 to 4 in the morning, the time she wakes. Night waking also counts when classifying severity.
Night symptoms point to vocal fold dysfunction

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic; night waking with cough and wheeze is a typical asthma pattern. Tell: asthma may be worse at night because bronchial reactivity peaks at 3 to 4 in the morning.
Her rescue inhaler wears off at night
Her symptoms come at a fixed early-morning hour. Tell: the nightly timing follows a circadian peak in bronchial reactivity at 3 to 4 in the morning.
Cardiac asthma is wheezing from decompensated heart failure, and a healthy 25-year-old has no heart failure. Tell: her waking at 3 in the morning matches the circadian peak in bronchial reactivity.

C.q: A 63-year-old woman hospitalized with coronavirus disease 2019 and hypoxemia is on dexamethasone, but over 24 hours she needs rapidly increasing oxygen. Which treatment should be added?
opts: Correct. Rapid progression in a hospitalized patient may warrant baricitinib or tocilizumab in addition to corticosteroids, along with appropriate oxygen or ventilatory support. Her rising oxygen needs on dexamethasone are that rapid progression.
Baricitinib or tocilizumab is added to corticosteroids, not used in their place. Tell: rapid progression escalates therapy on top of dexamethasone; stopping the steroid removes the core treatment.

Molnupiravir is an early outpatient alternative when preferred options are unsuitable, not a hospital escalation for hypoxemia. Tell: the escalation drugs for rapid progression are baricitinib or tocilizumab.

Antibacterial treatment is not used for coronavirus disease 2019 without a bacterial complication, and none is described. Tell: her worsening is viral and inflammatory progression, which baricitinib or tocilizumab addresses.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
C.q: What does a chest radiograph usually show in asthma?
opts: Effusions are not part of asthma; they suggest heart failure, infection or malignancy. The asthma radiograph is usually normal or hyperinflated. Tell: an effusion sits outside the lung in the pleural space, far from asthma's airway disease.

Hilar lymphadenopathy is not an asthma finding and suggests a granulomatous or malignant process. The asthma radiograph is usually normal or shows hyperinflation. Tell: asthma is an airway disease that leaves the hila and lymph nodes alone.

Correct. The chest radiograph in asthma is usually normal or may show hyperinflation from air trapping, so it supports rather than makes the diagnosis and mainly helps exclude other causes of symptoms.

Consolidation suggests pneumonia, an alveolar filling process. In asthma the radiograph is usually normal or shows hyperinflation. Tell: asthma traps air and makes the lungs look darker and larger, while consolidation makes a lobe white.

C.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
C.q: A 22-year-old man with mild persistent asthma well controlled on an inhaled corticosteroid dislikes inhalers and asks to switch to montelukast tablets alone. Which statement should guide the counseling?
opts: It works as well as his inhaled steroid

Leukotriene modifiers are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids when used alone, so the switch would trade a better controller for a weaker one. Tell: the tablet's role is add-on therapy or exercise-induced bronchospasm, not replacing the inhaled steroid.
It is less effective than his inhaled steroid

Correct. Montelukast is a leukotriene modifier with modest clinical benefit, useful as add-on therapy, and less effective than inhaled corticosteroids as monotherapy. His inhaled steroid is the preferred first-line treatment for persistent asthma.
It is a long-acting beta-2 agonist

Montelukast is a leukotriene modifier, not a beta-2 agonist. Long-acting beta-2 agonists such as salmeterol bronchodilate for up to 12 hours and must be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid. Tell: montelukast is a tablet; long-acting beta-2 agonists are inhaled.
It is a rescue medicine for attacks

Montelukast is a long-term control medicine; quick relief comes from a short-acting beta-2 agonist, which every patient needs. Tell: rescue medicines act within minutes on smooth muscle, while leukotriene modifiers are controllers.

C.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
C.q: An 84-year-old woman in hospice with metastatic cancer has air hunger (a distressing sense of not getting enough breath). Her saturation is 95%. Which therapy is a listed special indication?
opts: Correct. The hospice patient has air hunger, a distressing sense of not getting enough breath, and a saturation of 95%. Air hunger is a listed special indication, and symptom relief is a listed benefit of oxygen, so oxygen is given for comfort even without hypoxia.

An endotracheal tube is an advanced airway placed in the trachea. Her complaint is the sensation of breathlessness, and an airway device is not the listed therapy for it. Tell: air hunger is relieved by oxygen for symptom relief.
No oxygen, since saturation is normal

Normal saturation does not exclude oxygen here. Air hunger and cluster headache are the special indications, and symptom relief is a listed benefit. Tell: for air hunger the goal is relief of the sensation, so a reading of 95% does not settle it.
ruled out by a stated finding

A home oxygen qualification test documents hypoxia during rest, exertion or sleep using a saturation or arterial gas value. Her saturation is 95%, and the listed indication here is air hunger, not documented hypoxia. Tell: qualification documents hypoxia for home oxygen; air hunger is a special indication in itself.

C.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
C.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
C.q: What is the anion gap formula?
opts: Correct. The anion gap equals sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate, using serum electrolyte values. The normal anion gap is 9 to 15, and serum albumin accounts for most of it.
This drops bicarbonate, one of the two measured anions, and adds potassium. The formula is sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate). Tell: the gap subtracts both chloride and bicarbonate from sodium.

That is the Winter formula, which gives the expected carbon dioxide in metabolic acidosis. The anion gap is sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate). Tell: the Winter formula yields a carbon dioxide, the gap formula yields a gap.
This reverses the cation and the anions. The gap starts from sodium: sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate). Tell: the positive term is the measured cation, sodium.

C.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
C.q: A 72-year-old man with chronic lung disease is drowsy and confused, with asterixis (a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.22 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 75 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder best explains his findings?
opts: Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate, and his is 30, which is high. The high carbon dioxide drives his acidemia and his neurologic findings. Tell: drowsiness, confusion and asterixis come from carbon dioxide retention.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The pH of 7.22 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 75 is high and matches it, so it is respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate of 30 is the renal response. Somnolence, confusion and asterixis are its listed clinical findings, and chronic lung disease fits.

His bicarbonate is high, but his pH of 7.22 is low, and a primary metabolic alkalosis would raise the pH. The bicarbonate is renal compensation for the retained carbon dioxide. Tell: the pH direction names the primary disorder.
Respiratory alkalosis is a low carbon dioxide with a high pH. His carbon dioxide is 75 with a pH of 7.22, the reverse. Tell: asterixis and somnolence point to carbon dioxide retention.

C.q: A 59-year-old man with alcoholism and chronic liver disease has community-acquired pneumonia and is stable for outpatient treatment. He had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in the past. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: This is a comorbidity regimen, but amoxicillin-clavulanate contains the amoxicillin that caused his anaphylaxis. Tell: allergy history is reviewed first, and it removes this combination, so the respiratory fluoroquinolone is the remaining listed option.
ruled out by a stated finding

Doxycycline by itself is for outpatients without comorbidities. His alcoholism and chronic liver disease call for a combination or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: with comorbidities, doxycycline only partners a beta-lactam.
Amoxicillin by itself is for outpatients with no comorbidities, and he has alcoholism and liver disease as well as an amoxicillin allergy. Tell: two separate clues rule this option out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Alcoholism and chronic liver disease are listed comorbidities, so he needs a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). His amoxicillin anaphylaxis removes the amoxicillin-based combination, leaving the fluoroquinolone, with a review of QT, interactions and fluoroquinolone risks.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: What is the role of oral corticosteroids in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: After an admission the discharge bundle starts long-acting bronchodilators promptly and considers an inhaled corticosteroid if eosinophils are high. Tell: oral steroids treat the exacerbation, not the months after it.

Correct. Oral steroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, which is why they are missing from the list of common chronic therapies. Exacerbations are treated with antibiotics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids and oxygen.
Group B starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic. Tell: oral steroids are never chronic maintenance here; they are given for exacerbations.
Group A starts with a single bronchodilator, short- or long-acting. Tell: oral corticosteroids are reserved for acute exacerbations. Low-burden patients never need systemic steroids for maintenance.

D.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
D.q: A 31-year-old woman has spirometry for suspected asthma. Before a bronchodilator her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 61% predicted with a ratio of 55%; after albuterol it is 94% predicted, a 54% improvement. Which interpretation fits?
opts: Spirometry does depend on effort, and coaching helps, but poor effort would not produce a clear 54% rise after a bronchodilator. Tell: a large, consistent response to albuterol reflects reversible obstruction, not inconsistent effort.

Before the bronchodilator her 1-second volume was 61% predicted with a 55% ratio, both reduced, so the test is not normal. Tell: the pre-bronchodilator values show obstruction, and the post-bronchodilator values show it reversing.
ruled out by a stated finding

Fixed obstruction would barely change after a bronchodilator. Her 1-second volume rose by 54% of its starting value, from 61% to 94% predicted. Tell: a rise of 12% or more is the reversible pattern that supports asthma.

Correct. A reduced 1-second volume and a reduced ratio before the bronchodilator show airflow limitation, and a 54% improvement after albuterol, far above the 12% threshold, shows reversibility. A positive bronchodilator response strongly supports asthma.

D.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
D.q: A 47-year-old woman has asthma symptoms 3 days a week, wakes at night 3 times a month, and uses albuterol 3 days a week but not daily. She has minor limitation of activity. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 72% predicted with a ratio reduced by 4%. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Most of her features are mild persistent, but mild persistent requires a 1-second volume above 80%; hers is 72%. Severity follows the worst feature. Tell: lung function between 60% and 80% sets her one class higher.

Correct. Her symptoms, night waking, rescue use and minor limitation fit mild persistent, but a 1-second volume between 60% and 80% predicted (72%) is a moderate persistent feature, and severity follows the most severe category in which any feature occurs.

Intermittent asthma allows symptoms on 2 or fewer days a week and a 1-second volume above 80%. She has 3 days a week and 72% function. Tell: both her symptoms and her spirometry exceed the intermittent column.

Severe persistent asthma needs a 1-second volume below 60% or features such as symptoms throughout the day. Her worst feature, 72%, sits in the moderate band. Tell: 72% is above the 60% line that marks severe disease.

D.q: A 58-year-old man is admitted with coronavirus disease 2019. His oxygen saturation is 90% on room air, and he needs supplemental oxygen. Which medication is the core treatment?
opts: Molnupiravir is an outpatient adult alternative when the preferred early antivirals are unsuitable. It has no place in the hospital pathway for hypoxemia. Tell: hypoxemic inpatients get dexamethasone, with remdesivir considered.

Correct. Hospitalized adults with hypoxemia receive dexamethasone, usually for up to 10 days or until discharge, with remdesivir considered by timing and respiratory support. Oxygenation and severity, not simply a positive test or elapsed time, decide the pathway, and his saturation of 90% puts him on it.

Antibacterial treatment is withheld in coronavirus disease 2019 without a bacterial complication, which he does not have. Tell: the indicated pathway is antiviral and supportive care plus dexamethasone for hypoxemia, not an antibiotic.

Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir belongs to the early outpatient pathway for high-risk patients with mild or moderate disease and no hypoxemia. He is hypoxemic and admitted. Tell: hypoxemia moves the patient to the hospital pathway, built on dexamethasone.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 66-year-old woman being treated for community-acquired pneumonia becomes newly confused. Her heart rate is 118/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 87% on room air, and her urine output has fallen. Which complication has developed?
opts: Correct. When pneumonia becomes systemic it progresses toward bacteremia or septicemia: tachycardia with hypotension, hypoxia, confusion or altered mental status, and decreased urine output or kidney function. She has every one of those signs, which changes her site of care and urgency of support.

Empyema is suggested by dullness to percussion at the base of the lung, a local pleural complication that is drained when indicated. It does not by itself explain hypotension, confusion and falling urine output. Tell: her findings are systemic, not a local pleural sign.

Pleurisy is heard as a pleural rub, a local finding when the infection irritates the pleura. Her problem is circulatory failure with organ dysfunction. Tell: a rub is a chest sound; hypotension with confusion and low urine output is a systemic picture.

A lung abscess develops insidiously over weeks with foul sputum, hemoptysis and a cavity with an air-fluid level. Her change is acute, with signs of circulatory collapse. Tell: abscess is slow and local; septicemia is fast and systemic.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease uses his albuterol inhaler 10 to 12 times a day and has noticed palpitations and anxiety. Which explanation should guide counseling?
opts: Correct. Every patient should have albuterol, but it should not be used excessively because of toxicity and the risk of cardiac and psychiatric side effects. His heavy use also signals that his maintenance therapy and group need review.
Albuterol use is harmless at any amount
Excessive albuterol use carries toxicity with cardiac and psychiatric side effects, as his palpitations and anxiety suggest. Tell: rescue use is meant to be occasional, not constant.
Every patient should have an albuterol inhaler to prevent or reduce symptoms. Tell: the answer is less rescue use through better maintenance, not giving up the rescue inhaler.
His symptoms come from the antimuscarinic
Long-acting antimuscarinics are poorly absorbed, with mainly dry mouth. Tell: palpitations and anxiety with heavy albuterol use point to the beta agonist.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 59-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a mild exacerbation with increased breathlessness. She is alert, her vital signs are stable, she has no new signs, and her husband is at home with her. Which setting of care is most appropriate?
opts: Admission is for marked symptoms despite acute management, need for noninvasive ventilation, new signs, arrhythmia, poor secretion control, comorbidities, age or lack of resources. She has none. Tell: a mild, stable exacerbation stays outpatient.
Intensive care is for instability, major infection, invasive ventilation, sepsis, altered mental status or acidosis. Tell: an alert, stable patient with a mild exacerbation does not need it.

Noninvasive ventilation is for hypercapnic respiratory failure; nothing suggests failure here. Tell: her mild exacerbation is treated outpatient with bronchodilators, steroids and, if sputum changes, antibiotics.

Correct. More than 80% of exacerbations can be managed as outpatients. She meets no admission criterion: no marked symptoms despite treatment, no need for noninvasive ventilation, no new signs or arrhythmia, and support at home.

Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. D.q: What are amphoric breath sounds, heard with a lung abscess?
opts: A pleural rub may be heard in pneumonia when pleurisy develops. Tell: amphoric sounds are the open-jar sound of a cavity, low-pitched with high overtones.
A wheeze is a narrowed-airway sound, heard centrally in acute bronchitis. Tell: amphoric sounds come from air crossing a cavity and are low-pitched with high overtones.
Rhonchi that clear with coughing come from airway mucus, as in acute bronchitis. Tell: amphoric sounds come from a large open cavity and do not clear with a cough.

Correct. Amphoric breath sounds are low-pitched with some high-pitched overtones as air moves across a large open cavity, like breathing across an open jar. A lung abscess may also give dullness, whispered pectoriloquy and bronchophony.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
D.q: A 74-year-old man with long-standing heart disease has 3 days of worsening shortness of breath, swelling of both legs, and new wheezing. He has no history of asthma or allergies, and his wheeze began as his heart failure decompensated. Which explanation for his wheezing is most likely?
opts: Exercise-induced bronchospasm is common in children and adolescents and resolves within an hour of exercise. His wheeze is continuous over 3 days with edema. Tell: an older patient with edema and decompensated heart failure is the cardiac asthma setting.

Correct. Cardiac asthma is wheezing caused by decompensated heart failure. A 74-year-old with heart disease, leg swelling and wheeze that began with the decompensation, and no asthma or atopy, fits it; the heart failure, not the airway, needs treatment.

Intrinsic asthma does start in adulthood, but it is not tied to heart failure decompensation and usually comes with nasal polyps or aspirin sensitivity. Tell: wheeze appearing with leg swelling as the heart fails points to cardiac asthma.
Extrinsic asthma is atopic and allergen-triggered; he has no allergies or asthma history. Tell: the timing with his heart failure and the leg swelling identify a cardiac cause of wheezing.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 70-year-old woman with cirrhosis and an albumin of 1.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL) has a metabolic acidosis, a chloride of 110 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and an anion gap of 11 (normal 9 to 15). Which finding most limits how much the normal gap can reassure you?
opts: A high chloride marks a true normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis; it is a finding, not an error in the gap. Her low albumin is the listed source of error. Tell: hypoalbuminemia sits on the error list; chloride does not.

The acidosis is what the gap is meant to sort; it does not distort the number. Hypoalbuminemia does, by removing the anion that makes up most of the normal gap. Tell: look for the listed errors: low albumin, sodium extremes, antibiotics.

Correct. Albumin accounts for most of the normal anion gap, so hypoalbuminemia lowers the gap and can hide added unmeasured anions. A normal gap does not exclude a high-gap acidosis and should not override clinical concern.

Losing unmeasured cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium) raises the gap, so it would make a normal value less likely, not falsely reassuring. Her low albumin lowers it. Tell: fewer cations raise the gap; less albumin lowers it.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
D.q: A 15-year-old soccer player has cough, chest tightness and wheezing that start within 3 minutes after hard running, peak about 10 to 15 minutes later, and clear within an hour. She has no symptoms at rest or at night. Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Moderate persistent asthma brings daily symptoms and night awakenings more than once a week. She has none at rest or at night. Tell: symptoms tied only to exercise and gone within an hour fit exercise-induced bronchospasm.
ruled out by a stated finding

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic, but the pattern of onset within 3 minutes, a 10-to-15-minute peak and resolution by an hour is the exercise-induced bronchospasm timeline. Tell: the precise post-exercise timing is the decisive clue.

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is common in children and adolescents, begins during or within 3 minutes after exercise, peaks in 10 to 15 minutes and resolves by 60 minutes, exactly this player's pattern, with no symptoms at rest or at night.
Catamenial asthma follows the menstrual cycle. Her symptoms follow exercise, appearing within minutes and clearing within the hour. Tell: the trigger is running, not a point in a monthly cycle.

D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 37-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has worsening weakness and shallow, labored breathing over a day. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.27 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 57 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Chronic compensation would raise bicarbonate about 3.5 per 10 mm Hg, to about 30 here (57 is 17 above 40). Her 26 is the acute response to a one-day crisis. Tell: the kidneys have not had time, and a sudden onset signals acute.

Correct. The pH of 7.27 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 57 is high and matches it (respiratory). Bicarbonate rose only about 1 per 10 mm Hg (17 above 40 gives about 26), so it is acute. Myasthenia gravis is a listed neuromuscular cause of acute respiratory acidosis.
Her pH of 7.27 is low, so this cannot be an alkalosis. Her bicarbonate of 26 is inside the normal range, not high. Tell: metabolic alkalosis would need a high pH and a high bicarbonate.

Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate, and hers is 26, which is normal. The high carbon dioxide from weak, shallow breathing matches the acidemia. Tell: a normal bicarbonate with a high carbon dioxide means respiratory.
ruled out by a stated finding
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 22, 26, 59

D.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
D.q: A 71-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a stable chronic respiratory acidosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which serum electrolyte finding is expected?
opts: Hyperchloremia is the pattern of respiratory alkalosis compensation (kidneys retain chloride) and of normal-gap metabolic acidosis. His kidneys are excreting chloride. Tell: chronic respiratory acidosis is the low-chloride state.

His kidneys retain bicarbonate to offset the carbon dioxide; his is 33, high. A low bicarbonate marks metabolic acidosis or respiratory alkalosis compensation. Tell: the compensation for retained carbon dioxide is retained bicarbonate.

Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate, so hypochloremia accompanies the raised bicarbonate of 33. This is the renal compensation.
An elevated gap marks a metabolic acidosis with added unmeasured anions; his disorder is respiratory, with a high bicarbonate. Tell: the gap is a tool for metabolic acidosis.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

D.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
D.q: An 80-year-old man on home oxygen at 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier complains of a sore, dry nose and occasional bleeding. Which change addresses the cause?
opts: Correct. He is on 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier, and has a sore, dry nose with bleeding. That is mucosal irritation. Humidity is used with cannula flow rates greater than 4 L/min, so adding humidity to the oxygen treats the cause.

A non-rebreather mask is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. He has a sore nose, not worsening hypoxia, and the mask would not solve it. Tell: his problem is dryness at a flow above 4 L/min.
Raising the flow to 6 L/min keeps him above 4 L/min, where humidity is already needed and he has none. A higher flow leaves the missing humidity in place. Tell: fix the humidity, not the flow.
Apply a petroleum lip and nose balm

A petroleum-based balm is on the list of products to avoid with home oxygen, because oxygen is highly flammable. It would not be an appropriate treatment for his nose. Tell: petroleum products stay away from oxygen.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 24-year-old man with a panic attack is breathing fast, with perioral numbness and tingling hands. His roommate hands him a paper bag to breathe into. What is accurate education about the bag?
opts: It is unnecessary and may lower his oxygen

Correct. Breathing into a paper bag is not necessary for hyperventilation: it fails to correct the carbon dioxide and may decrease oxygen, and any benefit is placebo. Hyperventilation is usually self-limited, and the cause is treated.
It is needed to prevent tetany

Tetany can occur in severe respiratory alkalosis from low ionized calcium, but the bag does not prevent it; hyperventilation is usually self-limited. Tell: treat the cause, not the carbon dioxide with a bag.
It works by raising his bicarbonate
Rebreathing does not act on bicarbonate; bicarbonate changes come from the kidneys over hours to days. The bag's benefit is placebo. Tell: bicarbonate is renal and slow; no bag reaches it.
It safely corrects his carbon dioxide
The bag fails to correct carbon dioxide, and it may lower oxygen. Its effect is placebo. Tell: the paper bag fails on both counts, carbon dioxide and safety.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: Which neuromuscular disorders are listed as causes of acute respiratory acidosis?
opts: Pregnancy and hyperthyroidism are endocrine causes of respiratory alkalosis. The acute neuromuscular causes of respiratory acidosis are myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome. Tell: the stem asks for neuromuscular disorders, and these are endocrine.
Muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

Muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are the neuromuscular causes of chronic respiratory acidosis. The acute ones are myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome. Tell: acute and chronic have separate neuromuscular lists.

Salicylates and nicotine are toxic causes of respiratory alkalosis. Myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome cause acute respiratory acidosis. Tell: toxins that stimulate breathing lead to alkalosis, not acidosis.

Correct. Myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome are the listed neuromuscular causes of acute respiratory acidosis. Muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are the neuromuscular causes of the chronic form.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease had 3 moderate exacerbations in the past year. Her blood eosinophil count is 110. She is starting maintenance therapy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, not daily maintenance. Tell: exacerbation prevention comes from long-acting inhaled bronchodilators.
A single bronchodilator is the group A start, for low risk and few symptoms. Three exacerbations make her group E. Tell: high risk calls for both long-acting bronchodilators.
Adding an inhaled corticosteroid is considered in group E when eosinophils are 300 or more. Hers are 110. Tell: without that eosinophil count, the steroid's pneumonia risk is not justified.

Correct. Three moderate exacerbations make her high risk, group E, which starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic. Her eosinophil count of 110 is below 300, so an inhaled corticosteroid, with its pneumonia risk, is not added.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 34-year-old man explored a cave with heavy bat droppings 2 weeks ago. He now has high fever, chills, myalgias, a nonproductive cough, chest pain and a headache. Which test should be ordered?
opts: Chlamydia psittaci comes from birds such as parrots, parakeets and poultry, and its test is a respiratory nucleic acid test. His exposure was bats in a cave. Tell: match the test to the exposure; bats and soil point to histoplasmosis.

Serum cryptococcal antigen tests for Cryptococcus, which is inhaled from the environment and is a risk mainly with immunocompromise. His story is a bat-dropping exposure with an acute flu-like illness. Tell: bat droppings name Histoplasma.

Routine bacterial sputum culture is obtained selectively in community-acquired pneumonia and does not test for this fungus. Tell: the bat-dropping exposure points to a fungal antigen test, not a bacterial culture.

Correct. Exposure to bat droppings followed by fever, chills, myalgias, a dry cough, chest pain and headache within 3 to 17 days fits acute histoplasmosis. Testing uses the urine Histoplasma antigen, often with serum antigen and antibody tests.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
D.q: A 45-year-old man with newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis has a rapid molecular test showing rifampin resistance. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: The standard regimen relies on rifampin for all 6 months, so it is built for drug-susceptible disease. Tell: rifampin resistance takes the patient out of the standard pathway and into expert management.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ethambutol is already part of the initial phase and is stopped once isoniazid and rifampin susceptibility is shown. Tell: resistance needs rapid susceptibility testing and expert management, not one extra drug.
Rapid susceptibility testing and expert care

Correct. Rifampin resistance requires rapid susceptibility testing and expert management. Rifampin is one of the two drugs given through the whole 6-month standard regimen, so resistance to it takes him off the standard pathway.
The 17-week regimen is for susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis and contains rifapentine, a rifamycin. Tell: rifampin resistance rules out the susceptible-disease regimens; he needs expert management.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 65-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 55% predicted, a 6-minute walk distance of 160 meters, a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1, and a body mass index of 27. Based on his BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index, what is his estimated 4-year survival?
opts: About 18% belongs to scores of 7 to 10. His total is 3. Tell: his dyspnea grade of 1 and body mass index of 27 score nothing. His total of 3 is far below 7.
About 57% belongs to scores of 5 to 6, which would need 2 more points. Tell: his total is 1 (airflow) + 2 (walk) = 3. A total of 3 sits in the 3-to-4 band.

Correct. 1-second volume 55% (50 to 64) = 1 + walk 160 meters (150 to 249) = 2 + dyspnea grade 1 = 0 + body mass index 27 (over 21) = 0, for a total of 3. Scores of 3 to 4 predict about 67% 4-year survival.
About 80% needs a total of 0 to 2. His walk of 160 meters alone scores 2 and his 1-second volume adds 1. Tell: 3 points moves him to the 67% band. A walk of 150 to 249 meters costs him 2 points.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 38-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has 3 weeks of progressive shortness of breath on exertion, a nonproductive cough, fever and weight loss. His respiratory rate is 28/min, and his lungs sound nearly normal. A chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates spreading out from the perihilar regions. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mycoplasma is on the Pneumocystis differential, but it mostly affects school-age children and young adults in household or group outbreaks with gradual fever and a persistent cough. Tell: weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea in untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection point to the opportunistic fungus.

Correct. Untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection is the leading risk, and Pneumocystis is the most common opportunistic infection in that group. Progressive exertional dyspnea, a nonproductive cough, fever, a near-normal lung examination and diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates are its pattern.

Lobar pneumococcal pneumonia gives an acute illness with purulent sputum and a dense consolidation confined to one lobe, with crackles and dullness over it. His cough is dry, his lungs are quiet and his infiltrates are bilateral. Tell: perihilar and bilateral is the Pneumocystis film, not a lobar one.

Acute histoplasmosis follows inhaled soil or bird or bat droppings, with high fever, chills, myalgias, chest pain and headache 3 to 17 days after the exposure. No exposure is described. Tell: his story is defined by his immune status, not by an exposure history.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
D.q: A 42-year-old man with cough and weight loss has a sputum culture that identifies Mycobacterium bovis. How is this organism classified?
opts: Mycobacterium avium complex is a common cause of nontuberculous lung disease and is not part of the tuberculosis complex. Tell: bovis is grouped with tuberculosis and africanum; avium is grouped with kansasii and abscessus.

Slow and rapid growers are both found among the nontuberculous mycobacteria, which include many environmental species. Tell: Mycobacterium bovis is a tuberculosis complex member, and the complex's principal pathogen grows slowly.

The nontuberculous mycobacteria named are Mycobacterium avium complex, Mycobacterium kansasii and Mycobacterium abscessus, which are environmental species. Tell: Mycobacterium bovis sits inside the tuberculosis complex alongside Mycobacterium africanum.

Correct. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex causes tuberculosis; Mycobacterium tuberculosis is its principal human pathogen, and other members include Mycobacterium bovis and Mycobacterium africanum. Species identification matters because transmission and treatment differ from the nontuberculous mycobacteria.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 59-year-old man has been intubated and mechanically ventilated for 3 days after a motor vehicle crash. He develops a new fever, purulent endotracheal secretions and a new infiltrate. How should this pneumonia be classified?
opts: Community-acquired pneumonia is acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission. His began after 3 days on the ventilator. Tell: an infection that starts after more than 48 hours of intubation is not community acquired.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Ventilator-associated pneumonia develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and he has been ventilated for 3 days. Colonized secretions inhaled through the tube cause it, and it carries higher mortality and a longer intensive care stay.

The health care-associated category is retired and is no longer used to classify pneumonia or choose therapy. Tell: the current labels are community acquired, hospital acquired and ventilator associated, decided by setting and timing.

Hospital-acquired pneumonia is pneumonia 48 hours or more after admission; when it follows more than 48 hours of endotracheal intubation, the specific label is ventilator associated. Tell: the breathing tube decides the name.

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 45-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has worsening weakness and shallow breathing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 58 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is the priority treatment for his acid-base disorder?
opts: Correct. A high carbon dioxide with a low pH and a barely raised bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome is a listed neuromuscular cause. Acute respiratory acidosis is treated by restoring ventilation while the cause is treated.
Give sodium bicarbonate to raise the pH

His acidosis comes from retained carbon dioxide, so the fix is ventilation; therapy aimed at the pH itself is reserved for an unsustainable pH (below 6.7), alongside the cause. His pH is 7.26. Tell: respiratory acidosis is treated by breathing, not by bicarbonate.

Careful oxygen titration is the approach for chronic respiratory acidosis. His is acute (bicarbonate 26), and the priority is restoring ventilation. Tell: acute equals restore ventilation; chronic equals careful oxygen.

Renal compensation begins only after 6 to 12 hours, takes days, and never returns the pH to normal. His breathing is failing now. Tell: compensation alone never restores the pH; the disorder must be corrected.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for mycobacterial infections for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
D.q: Which age group is named as a higher-progression-risk group after tuberculosis infection?
opts: Older adults are noted to present atypically with pulmonary tuberculosis, but the age group on the progression list is infancy and young childhood. Tell: atypical presentation and progression risk are different points.

Correct. Infancy and young childhood are listed with the higher progression risks, alongside human immunodeficiency virus infection or major immunosuppression, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, transplantation, prolonged corticosteroids and recent infection within 2 years.
Early and middle adulthood are not listed as a progression risk group; infancy and young childhood are. Tell: risk is named at the start of life, not in the adult years.
Adolescence is not singled out as a progression risk; the age group listed is infancy and young childhood. Tell: the youngest children carry the higher risk.
D.cite: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx, Slides 15, 17

D.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
D.q: A 19-year-old man with newly diagnosed persistent asthma starts using a peak flow meter at home. During his first weeks of readings while well, what is the main purpose of the readings?
opts: Forced vital capacity is a spirometry measure; a peak flow meter records only the peak expiratory flow. Tell: home readings establish a personal best baseline and then assess control.
Diagnosis rests on spirometry before and after a bronchodilator; peak flow is a home monitoring tool. Tell: the early readings set his personal best, which the action-plan zones are built from.

Correct. Home peak flow monitoring first establishes a baseline for the patient, his personal best, and then assesses control against it. His action-plan zones are set as percentages of that personal best, so the early readings are the foundation.
Allergen triggers are identified by skin or blood allergy testing, not peak flow numbers. Tell: peak flow tracks airflow over time, and its first job is to establish his personal best.

D.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
D.q: A 27-year-old woman with diabetic ketoacidosis has a bicarbonate of 10 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L) and a carbon dioxide of 22 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). By the Winter formula, how is her respiratory compensation?
opts: Correct. Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23, plus or minus 2, so 21 to 25. Her measured 22 falls inside that range, so this is a simple, appropriately compensated metabolic acidosis.

An added respiratory acidosis would show a carbon dioxide above 25, the top of the Winter range for a bicarbonate of 10. Her 22 is within 21 to 25. Tell: above the range means too little compensation.
ruled out by a stated finding

An added respiratory alkalosis is not needed to explain her carbon dioxide: her 22 sits inside the expected 21 to 25, so compensation alone accounts for the fall. Tell: a value inside the Winter range is appropriate compensation.
ruled out by a stated finding
It cannot be judged without the gap

The anion gap types the acidosis but is not needed for the Winter check, which uses only the bicarbonate: 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23, plus or minus 2. Tell: compensation is judged from bicarbonate and carbon dioxide.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 58

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis and hepatic failure also has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and takes an antacid for heartburn. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which of his conditions best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Correct. High pH with a low carbon dioxide of 31 and a nearly normal bicarbonate is respiratory alkalosis. Hepatic failure is a listed cause of respiratory alkalosis; neither of his medicines lowers carbon dioxide.
Antacids cause a metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate above 26. His bicarbonate is 23, and his primary change is the low carbon dioxide. Tell: antacid alkalosis raises bicarbonate.
ruled out by a stated finding
Diabetic ketoacidosis is an elevated-gap metabolic acidosis with a low pH. His pH is 7.48, alkalemic. Tell: ketoacidosis lowers bicarbonate and pH.
Metformin causes an elevated-gap metabolic acidosis, a low pH with a low bicarbonate. His pH is 7.48. Tell: metformin drives the pH down.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: Alongside clinical judgment, which tool is preferred to support the admission decision in community-acquired pneumonia?
opts: Correct. The Pneumonia Severity Index plus clinical judgment is preferred for admission decisions; the five-item confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age score complements it but does not replace clinical judgment.

A white blood cell count alone does not set the place of care, and routine blood counts do not help every stable outpatient. Tell: the admission decision uses the Pneumonia Severity Index with judgment.
Sputum cultures are selective, for severe disease or resistant-pathogen risk, and their results come too late to decide admission. Tell: the Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment guides disposition.
The chest radiograph confirms that pneumonia is present but is not the preferred admission tool. Tell: the place of care is chosen with the Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: A 67-year-old man has a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.55 and a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 34% predicted. Which airflow grade fits?
opts: Grade 1, mild, needs 80% predicted or more; at 34% he is far below. Tell: grade 1 is near-normal airflow, and he has about a third of predicted. His ratio confirms obstruction; the grade then depends on the 1-second volume.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted; 34% is below that range. Tell: under 50% the grade is at least severe. Moderate means at least half of predicted airflow, which he does not have.
Correct. With the ratio below 0.70, the grade comes from the post-bronchodilator 1-second volume: 34% sits in the 30% to 49% band, grade 3, severe. Grade 4 would need less than 30%.
Grade 4, very severe, is below 30% predicted. At 34% he is just above that cutoff. Tell: 30% to 49% is grade 3, so 34% stays severe. A 4-point margin still counts; the bands do not round.

D.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
D.q: A 71-year-old man starting home oxygen asks why he must be so careful at home if oxygen is "just air." Which property of oxygen underlies the safety teaching?
opts: Oxygen does not turn into carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide appears in the teaching only as a reason for working carbon monoxide alarms. Tell: alarms detect carbon monoxide; flammability is the property of oxygen.
Oxygen being heavier than water is not a property stated and has no bearing on the teaching. The reason for the care is that oxygen is highly flammable. Tell: the key property is flammability.
It is toxic to breathe for visitors
Oxygen is not described as toxic to visitors. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction. Tell: the home safety teaching rests on flammability.

Correct. Oxygen is highly flammable, which is why home oxygen teaching includes no smoking in the home, staying away from heat sources, avoiding petroleum products and posting signs. Oxygen is not just air, and fire is a listed hazard.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
D.q: A 74-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation takes a long-acting beta agonist, a long-acting antimuscarinic and an inhaled corticosteroid; he rarely uses albuterol. His atrial fibrillation episodes and palpitations have become more frequent since his regimen was started. Which component is most likely contributing?
opts: Excessive albuterol carries cardiac risk, but he rarely uses it. Tell: the daily long-acting beta agonist delivers continuous sympathetic stimulation, the likelier cause.
ruled out by a stated finding
The inhaled corticosteroid's listed risks in older adults are pneumonia and fractures, not arrhythmias. Tell: palpitations and more atrial fibrillation point to the beta agonist.
Long-acting antimuscarinics are poorly absorbed, and their adverse effects are limited mainly to dry mouth. Tell: worsening atrial fibrillation fits the sympathetic stimulation of the beta agonist.

Correct. Long-acting beta agonists produce sympathetic stimulation that can cause tachycardia and arrhythmias and can make atrial fibrillation worse; their cardiac effects are a listed concern in older adults. With rare albuterol use, the daily beta agonist is the likely driver.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 63-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a daytime resting oxygen saturation of 94% and normal saturation while walking, but overnight oximetry shows saturations of 86% at night only. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Nighttime desaturation is not ignored; it prompts evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea and other causes. Tell: night-only desaturation has its own branch of the oxygen pathway.
Exertional oxygen is for desaturation to 88% or less with exercise, and his saturation stays normal while walking. Tell: his only drop is overnight, which points to a sleep evaluation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Desaturation to 88% or less at night only calls for evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea and screening for other causes, rather than long-term oxygen. His daytime resting and exertional saturations are normal.
Long-term oxygen over 15 hours a day
Long-term oxygen for more than 15 hours a day is for severe resting desaturation while awake, 88% or less. His daytime resting value is 94%. Tell: night-only drops lead to a sleep evaluation first.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
D.q: A 73-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is ready for discharge after his treatment is optimized. His resting saturation on room air is 87%, and he has no pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure from lung disease) or high hematocrit. How often will his home oxygen be recertified?
opts: An interval of every 1 month is not one of the stated intervals. The two are 12 months for Group I and 3 months for Group II. Tell: only 12 months and 3 months appear as recertification intervals, and his criteria give 12.

Every 3 months applies to Group II, the conditional group with a saturation of 89% plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%. He has none of those and a saturation of 87% qualifies him as Group I. Tell: earlier recertification goes with a chronic complication.

Correct. His resting room-air saturation is 87%, at or below 88%, which is the Group I qualification (conditional Group II needs a comorbidity such as pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%). Group I patients are recertified every 12 months.

An interval of every 24 months is not stated either; Group I is recertified at 12 months and Group II at 3 months. Tell: with an uncomplicated resting saturation of 87%, the answer is the longer listed interval, 12 months.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
D.q: A 27-year-old woman with no known tuberculosis risk factors has a tuberculin skin test for a school requirement. At 48 hours a trained reader measures 12 mm of transverse induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for an early negative result after a recent exposure, and she has had none. Tell: a skin test reading in millimeters is compared with her risk group's cut-off, which gives a clear answer.

5 mm is reserved for human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. Tell: none of these applies to her, so the 15 mm cut-off is used.

Correct. With no known tuberculosis risk factors, her cut-off is 15 mm, the highest of the three thresholds. 12 mm of induration is below 15 mm, so the result is negative for her, even though it would be positive for someone in the 5 mm or 10 mm groups.
10 mm is for increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings or age under 5. Tell: she has no known risk factors, which puts her at 15 mm, and 12 mm falls short.

D.q: A 20-year-old college student has had 10 days of gradual fever, a persistent cough and headache. Several students in her dormitory have the same illness, and a respiratory nucleic acid test is positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. She has taken amoxicillin for 3 days without improvement. Which change is most appropriate?
opts: A longer course of an ineffective drug cannot help: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so beta-lactams do not work at any duration. Tell: her lack of response is expected, and the fix is a macrolide or doxycycline.

Correct. Beta-lactams are ineffective against Mycoplasma because it lacks a cell wall, so amoxicillin cannot work. Adults with Mycoplasma infection are treated with a macrolide such as azithromycin or with doxycycline, and a respiratory fluoroquinolone is an alternative.
Cefpodoxime is another beta-lactam, and beta-lactams are ineffective against Mycoplasma because it lacks a cell wall. Tell: change the drug class to a macrolide or doxycycline.

Adding clavulanate makes amoxicillin-clavulanate, still a beta-lactam. Mycoplasma has no cell wall for any beta-lactam to act on. Tell: the failure is a drug-class mismatch, not resistance that a beta-lactamase inhibitor could fix.

D.q: A 52-year-old woman with acute bronchitis was managed with supportive care 10 days ago and at first improved. She now returns with a new temperature of 102.2°F, shortness of breath and crackles at the left base. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: The 2 to 3 week cough applies to an uncomplicated course; improvement followed by worsening, new fever and dyspnea are return precautions that mean the course is no longer uncomplicated. Tell: reassurance fits a steady cough, not a relapse with fever.
ruled out by a stated finding

Codeine combinations are avoided routinely for limited benefit and risks of sedation, respiratory depression and misuse, and they do nothing for a new fever with focal crackles. Tell: her problem is a possible new diagnosis, not cough control.

Fever or focal findings should prompt evaluation for pneumonia rather than empiric bronchitis antibiotics; an antibiotic without a diagnosis skips the step that decides the regimen. Tell: new crackles with fever call for imaging first.

Correct. Worsening after initial improvement, fever and dyspnea are return precautions, and fever or focal findings prompt evaluation for pneumonia rather than empiric bronchitis antibiotics. A worsening cough means reconsidering the diagnosis, and suspected pneumonia is confirmed with chest radiography.

D.topic: Flow rates and fraction of inspired oxygen
D.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
D.q: Above what fraction of inspired oxygen is an air-entrainment nebulizer not recommended?
opts: 0.30 is below the recommended limit, which is not recommended above 0.50. At 0.30 the device would be used well within its recommended range. Tell: the ceiling is 0.50.
Correct. An air-entrainment nebulizer can deliver higher fractions of inspired oxygen, but use above 0.50 is not recommended. The recommended ceiling is 0.50, which corresponds to 50%.
0.80 is above the recommended ceiling. The device can deliver higher fractions, but use above 0.50 is not recommended. Tell: the recommended limit is 0.50, not 0.80.
1.0 is the top of the printed range for this device, not the recommended ceiling. Delivery above 0.50 is not recommended. Tell: the device can reach high fractions but is not recommended above 0.50.

D.q: Where in the United States is Histoplasma capsulatum mainly found?
opts: Travel to or residence in the Middle East is linked with Middle East respiratory syndrome. Tell: Histoplasma lives in the soils of the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys.
Southeast and East Asia are linked with avian influenza and severe acute respiratory syndrome. Tell: Histoplasma is a United States central and eastern fungus.
Travel to or residence in the southwestern United States is linked with Coccidioides and Hantavirus. Tell: Histoplasma centers on the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys.

Correct. In the United States the fungus is mainly found in the central and eastern states, especially the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, and it is acquired from soils with bird or bat droppings.

D.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: Sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106) and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26). What is the calculated anion gap?
opts: 12 is the bicarbonate value itself, not the gap. The gap is 140 - (104 + 12) = 24. Tell: the answer comes from the subtraction, not a single listed value.

Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 140 - (104 + 12) = 140 - 116 = 24. That is above the normal 9 to 15, so this is an elevated anion gap, as expected with such a low bicarbonate.
36 comes from 140 - 104 without subtracting the bicarbonate. The gap subtracts chloride and bicarbonate: 140 - 116 = 24. Tell: both anions are subtracted.
48 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (140 - 104 + 12). The correct arithmetic is 140 - (104 + 12) = 24. Tell: chloride and bicarbonate are added together first and the sum is subtracted.

D.q: A 57-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is intubated for respiratory failure and admitted to the intensive care unit. He has no validated risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy is an option for nonsevere inpatient pneumonia. Severe pneumonia uses a beta-lactam combination regimen. Tell: once a patient is ventilated, a beta-lactam must be part of the regimen.

Correct. Mechanical ventilation makes this severe community-acquired pneumonia, treated with a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas coverage is added only for validated risks, which he lacks; cultures are obtained and therapy de-escalated later.

Vancomycin covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and cefepime covers Pseudomonas, but severity alone does not mandate that coverage. Tell: severity changes the site of care and regimen, not automatic broad-spectrum coverage, and he has no validated risk.
A beta-lactam by itself leaves out the partner drug: severe pneumonia is treated with a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: severe means a combination regimen.

D.q: How is exercise-induced bronchospasm best prevented?
opts: A long-acting beta-2 agonist must not be used as monotherapy because it has no anti-inflammatory effect. Regular inhaled corticosteroids are the best prevention. Tell: any long-acting agent in asthma must ride with an inhaled corticosteroid.
ruled out by a stated finding

Theophylline is rarely used because of toxicity and is not the exercise strategy. Regular inhaled corticosteroids best prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm, with a short-acting inhaler before exercise. Tell: the pre-exercise drug is inhaled, not an oral methylxanthine.
A goal of asthma care is no limitation on activity; medication, not avoidance, prevents the bronchospasm. Tell: the treatment plan protects participation in sport rather than removing it.

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise and is best prevented with regular inhaled corticosteroid use. It is common in children and adolescents, so this keeps teenagers in sport.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: Which process is listed as a contributor to airway remodeling and parenchymal destruction in this disease?
opts: Surfactant is not among the listed contributors. Tell: the 3 listed drivers are chronic inflammation, oxidative stress and protease-antiprotease imbalance.
Smooth muscle spasm that reverses describes asthma's bronchoconstriction. Tell: this disease causes chronic, irreversible obstruction through remodeling and destruction, not spasm alone.

Immunoglobulin E binding to mast cells is the allergic pathway of extrinsic asthma. Tell: this disease is driven by inflammation, oxidative stress and an imbalance between proteases and antiproteases.

Correct. Airway remodeling and parenchymal destruction are driven by chronic inflammation, oxidative stress and protease-antiprotease imbalance. That imbalance is also why a lack of alpha-1 antitrypsin, a protease inhibitor, destroys the lung.

D.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
D.q: A 21-year-old woman in diabetic ketoacidosis has Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid breathing). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.22 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 20 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What does her breathing pattern accomplish?
opts: It is a primary respiratory alkalosis

A primary respiratory alkalosis would raise the pH above 7.45. Hers is 7.22, so her low carbon dioxide is compensation for the metabolic acidosis. Tell: low carbon dioxide with a low pH is compensation.
It retains carbon dioxide to raise her pH
Retaining carbon dioxide would lower the pH; it is how the lungs compensate a metabolic alkalosis. Deep, rapid breathing removes carbon dioxide. Tell: fast, deep breathing lowers carbon dioxide.

Impending respiratory failure is suggested when carbon dioxide is higher than the Winter formula predicts (1.5 x 8 + 8 = 20, plus or minus 2). Hers is 20, right on target. Tell: a tiring patient's carbon dioxide drifts up, not down.
It lowers carbon dioxide to offset the acidosis

Correct. Metabolic acidosis is compensated by increased ventilation to decrease carbon dioxide; in severe cases hyperventilation is profound, as Kussmaul respirations (increased tidal volume and tachypnea) in diabetic ketoacidosis. Her carbon dioxide of 20 shows it.

D.q: A 45-year-old man with uncomplicated influenza is going home with supportive care. Which development should prompt him to return urgently?
opts: Correct. Return precautions for influenza are shortness of breath, chest pain, dehydration, confusion, or improvement followed by worsening. A relapse after improving can signal a secondary bacterial pneumonia, a known complication of influenza.
A cough lasting past one week

Fever and systemic symptoms often improve over several days, but cough and fatigue may persist. Tell: a lingering cough by itself is expected; the urgent triggers are shortness of breath, chest pain, dehydration, confusion or a relapse.
Fever of 100°F to 104°F is part of influenza itself, and a low-grade fever on day 2 is expected. Tell: fever early in the illness is not a warning sign; worsening after improvement is.

Cough and fatigue may persist after the fever settles, so lingering tiredness is part of the expected course. Tell: return precautions focus on breathing, chest pain, fluids, mental status and a relapse after improvement.

D.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
D.q: A 33-year-old woman with asthma wakes with cough and mild wheeze. Her peak flow is 70% of her personal best, placing her in the yellow zone of her written action plan. What does the plan direct her to do first?
opts: Add quick-relief medicine and keep her controller

Correct. In the yellow zone, 50% to 79% of personal best, asthma is getting worse: she adds quick-relief medicine (a short-acting beta-2 agonist) and keeps taking her green-zone controller. An oral steroid is added only if she does not return to green after an hour.
Stop her controller until she feels better

The yellow zone keeps the green-zone controller going while adding quick relief; stopping it removes her anti-inflammatory treatment as she worsens. Tell: the plan adds medicine in the yellow zone, it never subtracts.
Start an oral steroid right away

The oral steroid enters the yellow-zone plan second, if her symptoms and peak flow do not return to green within an hour of quick-relief treatment. Tell: the first yellow-zone step is quick-relief medicine plus her usual controller.

Going to the hospital belongs to the red zone and the danger signs, such as trouble walking or talking from breathlessness or blue lips. At 70% with mild symptoms she is in yellow. Tell: yellow means add quick relief and keep the controller.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
D.q: A 29-year-old man is diagnosed with latent tuberculosis infection after a normal clinical evaluation. He lives with his newborn daughter and asks whether he could pass the infection to her. Which statement is accurate?
opts: He is contagious until his treatment ends

Contagiousness comes from pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols, not from latent infection. Tell: he is not infectious before, during or after his preventive treatment, which aims at the infection in his own body.
He is contagious when he coughs or sings

Coughing, speaking or singing releases infectious aerosols from pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis disease. Tell: latent infection has no active disease in his lungs or larynx, so he cannot spread it even when he coughs.
Latent infection does not spread to others

Correct. People with latent tuberculosis infection are infected but asymptomatic, are not infectious and cannot spread the disease; latent infection does not cause transmission. Spread comes from infectious aerosols released by pulmonary or laryngeal disease during coughing, speaking or singing.
He can spread it through close household contact

Close contact raises exposure risk only when the source has infectious tuberculosis disease, which a person with latent infection does not have. Tell: the source in household spread is someone with pulmonary or laryngeal disease.
