D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 41-year-old woman with Crohn disease has had profuse watery diarrhea for five days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.31 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Correct. The pH of 7.31 is acidemia, and the bicarbonate of 15 is low and matches it: metabolic. Gap = 137 - (112 + 15) = 10, within 9 to 15, with a high chloride, so it is a normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis. Bicarbonate loss in diarrhea fits.
Respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide, and hers is 31, which is low. The low bicarbonate of 15 is what matches the acidemia. Tell: her low carbon dioxide is respiratory compensation.
ruled out by a stated finding

The gap is 137 - (112 + 15) = 10, inside 9 to 15, so it is normal, not elevated. Her high chloride of 112 is the hyperchloremic pattern of the normal-gap type. Tell: elevated-gap acidosis is normochloremic, and her chloride is high.
ruled out by a stated finding
Metabolic alkalosis is a high pH with a high bicarbonate. Hers is 7.31 with a bicarbonate of 15, the reverse on both. Tell: diarrhea loses bicarbonate, which lowers it.

D.q: A 36-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus infection starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Her arterial oxygen pressure on room air is 61 mm Hg. Which therapy should be added?
opts: Correct. Adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated in Pneumocystis pneumonia linked to human immunodeficiency virus when the room-air arterial oxygen pressure is below 70 mm Hg, and hers is 61. Prednisone is started as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of starting treatment.

Her room-air arterial oxygen pressure of 61 mm Hg is below the threshold of 70, which is exactly when adjunctive steroids are indicated. Tell: compare the stated value with 70 mm Hg; below it, a steroid is added as early as possible.

The adjunct is a systemic corticosteroid, prednisone, given over 21 days; an inhaled steroid does not provide it. Tell: the room-air oxygen below 70 mm Hg calls for systemic prednisone started early, not an inhaler.

Pentamidine is an alternative to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, not an add-on for low oxygen. Deterioration is reassessed for toxicity, coinfection or failure rather than met with an automatic switch. Tell: her oxygen value triggers a steroid, not a second antimicrobial.

D.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
D.q: A 58-year-old woman with asthma and nasal polyps developed wheezing, facial flushing and a runny nose within an hour of taking aspirin last year. She now has painful knee osteoarthritis and asks for an anti-inflammatory pain reliever. Which drug is the most appropriate choice?
opts: Diclofenac is on the list of non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs to avoid in aspirin-sensitive asthma, and her flushing and wheeze after aspirin show that sensitivity. Tell: selective agents such as celecoxib are the ones she may use.

Correct. Her wheeze, flushing and rhinorrhea after aspirin mark aspirin-sensitive asthma, so non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs must be avoided. Selective agents such as celecoxib or meloxicam may be used, which treats her knee pain without the cross-reaction.

Naproxen is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, and patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma cross-react with that group. Her past aspirin reaction rules it out. Tell: the safe choices for her are the selective agents, celecoxib and meloxicam.

Indomethacin is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, the group that worsens aspirin-sensitive asthma, so her aspirin reaction rules it out. Tell: only the selective agents (celecoxib, meloxicam) are allowed in aspirin-sensitive asthma.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: A 64-year-old woman completes the 8-item symptom assessment test, each item scored 0 to 5: cough 2, phlegm 1, chest tightness 1, breathlessness on a hill or flight of stairs 3, limitation of home activities 2, confidence leaving home 1, sleep 1, and energy 2. What is her total score?
opts: Eleven drops 2 points, as if the energy item (2) were left out. Tell: all 8 items count, so add energy back: 11 + 2 = 13. Either way, her total of 13 is above the line of 10.
Twelve misses 1 point, as if one of the 1-point items (phlegm, chest tightness, confidence or sleep) were skipped. Tell: there are four 1-point items, and all of them count.

Correct. Cough 2 + phlegm 1 + chest tightness 1 + breathlessness on stairs 3 + home activities 2 + confidence leaving home 1 + sleep 1 + energy 2 = 13. A total of 10 or more counts as more symptoms when assigning her group.

Fourteen adds a point that is not there, as if breathlessness on stairs were scored 4 instead of 3. Tell: recheck each item; the correct sum is 13. An extra point would not change her group, but it is not the sum.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
D.q: Between exacerbations, the physical examination of a patient with asthma is often what?
opts: Correct. The examination may be normal between exacerbations, which is why an objective lung function measurement is needed for the diagnosis. Extrinsic asthma may still show nasal mucosal swelling, increased secretions, eczema or nasal polyps.

A barrel chest from chronic hyperinflation is the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease picture. The asthma exam is often normal between attacks. Tell: a persistent barrel chest implies fixed air trapping, which asthma usually does not have.

Wheezing usually appears during exacerbations; between attacks the exam is often normal because the obstruction is reversible. Tell: fixed, constant findings suggest irreversible disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease rather than asthma between attacks.

Clubbing is not an asthma finding; it suggests another chronic lung or heart disease. Between exacerbations the asthma examination may be entirely normal. Tell: asthma's reversible airway disease leaves no permanent marks such as clubbing.

D.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
D.q: A 66-year-old man on home oxygen restores old cars in his garage and rubs grease off his hands with an oil-based cleanser while wearing his cannula. Which teaching applies?
opts: Use a Venturi mask when working

A Venturi mask is a high flow device that gives a precise fraction, often used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It would not remove the petroleum product hazard. Tell: the teaching concerns what touches the oxygen, not which mask he wears.
Turn the flow up while working

Turning the flow up does not remove the petroleum product; the teaching is to avoid petroleum-based oils and grease, not to change the flow. Tell: the fix is to change the product, not the oxygen setting.
Wear a simple mask in the garage

A simple mask is a low flow device for mild to moderate respiratory distress. He has no respiratory problem described, and changing the mask would not address the grease. Tell: his hazard is the product on his hands.

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to avoid petroleum-based products such as lip balms, lotions, oils and grease. He is wearing his cannula while rubbing grease off with an oil-based cleanser, so he should avoid those petroleum oils and grease.

D.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
D.q: A 35-year-old man has had stable, well-controlled asthma for 2 years. How often should his spirometry be repeated to monitor progression?
opts: Monthly spirometry is far more often than needed for stable disease; home peak flow readings handle frequent monitoring. Tell: office spirometry for monitoring is repeated once a year.

Repeating spirometry every 3 months is more often than recommended for monitoring stable asthma. Tell: the interval for monitoring progression with spirometry is annual, while peak flow covers day-to-day control.

Correct. Spirometry is best done before and after a short-acting bronchodilator and is repeated annually to monitor progression. For this man with stable, controlled disease, a yearly test tracks his lung function between routine follow-up visits.
A 5-year gap is too long; spirometry is repeated annually to monitor progression. Tell: once a year is the monitoring interval, so 5 years would miss changes in his lung function.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
D.q: A 14-year-old girl with moderate persistent asthma comes in for her yearly influenza vaccine, and her mother asks whether she can have the nasal spray form instead of a shot. Which vaccine form calls for caution in her?
opts: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended in asthma because influenza can trigger exacerbations, so she should be vaccinated. Tell: the caution is about one form, the intranasal vaccine, not influenza vaccination itself.

Correct. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended because vaccine-preventable illness can trigger asthma exacerbations, but intranasal influenza vaccines call for caution, since they can be associated with exacerbation in younger patients such as this 14-year-old.

Vaccination is part of asthma care because vaccine-preventable illness can trigger exacerbations; being on controllers is not a reason to delay it. Tell: the one caution named is the intranasal influenza vaccine in younger patients.
Pneumonia vaccination is recommended for adults with asthma, and it is not the form that carries a caution. Tell: the caution applies to the intranasal influenza vaccine in younger patients.

D.q: A 66-year-old woman with a lung abscess has had two episodes of Clostridioides difficile colitis in the past year. Which part of a lung abscess plan should be avoided for her?
opts: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate follows the intravenous phase in the usual lung abscess plan. Tell: the drug flagged for Clostridioides difficile risk is clindamycin, so this oral step remains part of her treatment.

Correct. Clindamycin is reserved for selected alternatives because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and she has had two episodes of that colitis. Her abscess is treated with a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor instead, intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam is the usual first choice for lung abscess. Tell: her colitis history is the reason clindamycin, the drug held back for its Clostridioides difficile risk, is the one to avoid; this beta-lactam combination stays.

Lung abscess treatment commonly lasts several weeks, guided by clinical and radiographic response, and her colitis history does not change that. Tell: the history changes which drug is avoided, not how long the abscess is treated.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: Smoking-related emphysema typically follows which pattern?
opts: Correct. Emphysema from smoking is centrilobular and predominantly in the upper lobes. The panlobular, lower-lobe pattern belongs to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which is why basilar emphysema prompts testing for it.
Fibrosis is a restrictive change and, with silica or fiberglass, a different condition. Tell: smoking-related emphysema is an obstructive, upper-lobe, centrilobular destruction of airspaces.
Panlobular emphysema in the lower lobes is the alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency pattern. Tell: smoking damages the upper lobes in a centrilobular pattern.

Bronchial wall thickening is the imaging change of chronic bronchitis, an airway disease, not an emphysema pattern. Tell: smoking-related emphysema destroys centrilobular airspaces in the upper lobes.

D.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
D.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is on a Venturi mask set at 28%. His saturation is still below his target, and he is comfortable and alert. Which adjustment raises his fraction precisely?
opts: Correct. A Venturi mask changes its fraction through different ports (24-50% when flow is adjusted from 4-10 L/min). He is stable and comfortable at 28% but below his target, so the precise adjustment is a higher-fraction port. It keeps the fraction fixed.
Switch to a nasal cannula at 2 L/min

A nasal cannula at 2 L/min delivers about 28%, which is the fraction he is already getting, and it varies with his breathing. It would not raise his fraction precisely. Tell: a cannula varies with breathing; a Venturi port is fixed.
Add a reservoir bag to the mask

A reservoir bag converts a mask into a non-rebreather, which varies with demand and is for severe hypoxia. Adding one to a Venturi mask would not give a precise fraction. Tell: ports set a fixed fraction; a bag raises the fraction unpredictably.
Switch to a non-rebreather at 15 L/min

A non-rebreather at 15 L/min would jump to 60-100% and vary with his demand. He is alert and comfortable with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, so he needs a small, precise step. Tell: the Venturi mask adjusts in small fixed steps; the non-rebreather jumps.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
D.q: An 81-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia is alert and oriented. Her blood urea nitrogen is 17 mg/dL, respiratory rate 34/min and blood pressure 132/56 mm Hg. What is her CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score?
opts: A total of 1 counts age alone. She also has a respiratory rate of 34, which is 30 or more, and a diastolic pressure of 56, which is 60 or lower. Tell: tachypnea of 30 or more and either low pressure reading each add a point.

A total of 2 misses the blood pressure point. Low blood pressure scores for a systolic below 90 or a diastolic of 60 or lower, and her diastolic is 56. Tell: a normal systolic pressure does not cancel a low diastolic one.

Correct. Confusion 0 + urea 0 (17 is not above 20) + respiratory rate 1 (34 is 30 or more) + blood pressure 1 (a diastolic of 56 is 60 or lower, even with a normal systolic) + age 1 (81) = 3. That is high severity, with a risk of death of 15 to 40%: hospital and urgent senior review.
A total of 4 would add urea, but her blood urea nitrogen of 17 mg/dL is not above 20. Tell: the urea point needs more than 20 mg/dL, so she has three points, not four.

D.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
D.q: A 45-year-old man gets hives whenever he eats eggs and asks whether he can receive this season's influenza vaccine. He has never reacted to an influenza vaccine. What is the most appropriate plan?
opts: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone aged 6 months or older without a contraindication, and egg allergy is not a contraindication. Tell: skipping leaves him unprotected for no reason.

Specialist supervision applies to a severe reaction to a prior influenza vaccine, where an alternate vaccine may be possible. He has never reacted to one. Tell: his allergy is to eggs, which needs only routine safety steps.

Correct. Egg allergy does not require an egg-free product or precautions beyond routine vaccine safety measures. He has never reacted to an influenza vaccine, so he receives an age- and health-appropriate vaccine this season like any other adult.
An egg-free product is not required for egg allergy; any age- and health-appropriate vaccine may be used with routine safety measures. Tell: egg allergy changes nothing about product choice.

E.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin received several liters of normal saline during abdominal surgery. He has had no diarrhea. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 33 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 141 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 114 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which explains this blood gas?
opts: Metformin causes an elevated-gap acidosis, above 15. His gap is 141 - (114 + 17) = 10, and his chloride is high. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride points to the normal-gap list.
Hypoventilation raises carbon dioxide above 44; his is 33, lowered as compensation (Winter: 1.5 x 17 + 8 = 33.5). Tell: the low bicarbonate, not the carbon dioxide, matches his pH.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Low pH with a low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis; the gap is 141 - (114 + 17) = 10, within 9 to 15, with a high chloride: a normal-gap, hyperchloremic acidosis. Saline infusion is a listed normal-gap cause (chloride retention).
Diabetic ketoacidosis raises the gap with ketones; his gap of 10 is normal and his chloride high. Tell: ketoacidosis belongs to the elevated-gap mnemonic.

E.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
E.q: A 57-year-old man with severe obesity and a high fever from pneumonia has a carbon dioxide of 62 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). What usually causes a raised carbon dioxide like his?
opts: Hyperventilation increases excretion and lowers carbon dioxide (hypocapnia). His is raised. Tell: hypercapnia is under-breathing, hypocapnia over-breathing.
Excess bicarbonate retained by the kidneys
Retained bicarbonate is compensation for a raised carbon dioxide; it does not raise the carbon dioxide itself. Tell: carbon dioxide is set by ventilation, bicarbonate by the kidneys.

Correct. Hypercapnia is usually the result of under-excretion (hypoventilation), not excess production. At steady state carbon dioxide production matches excretion, so a high level means ventilation is not keeping up.
Fever increases carbon dioxide production, but hypercapnia is usually from under-excretion, not excess production; normal breathing clears the extra. Tell: blame the breathing first.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: Which presentation separates pneumonia from acute bronchitis?
opts: A low-grade fever with chills, body aches and fatigue is the cold-like start of acute bronchitis. Tell: pneumonia brings higher fevers and a faster breathing rate.
A central, substernal wheeze over the bronchial airways is a feature of acute bronchitis. Tell: pneumonia shows focal findings such as crackles, dullness or consolidation, with tachypnea.

Correct. Apart from walking pneumonia, pneumonia presents more severely than bronchitis: higher fevers and chills, pleuritic or atypical chest pain, a productive cough and shortness of breath with tachypnea. Bronchitis tends to bring a low-grade fever.
Colored sputum occurs in both and does not separate viral from bacterial illness. Tell: severity (higher fever, tachypnea, focal findings) is what points to pneumonia.

E.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
E.q: A 70-year-old woman on a nasal cannula at 6 L/min without humidification develops nosebleeds and a sore, crusted nose. Which hazard of oxygen therapy is this?
opts: Vasoconstriction is the listed concern with oxygen in a myocardial infarction. She has no cardiac event, and her findings are local nasal bleeding and crusting. Tell: vasoconstriction belongs with a myocardial infarction; dry, bleeding nasal mucosa belongs with mucosal irritation.

Hypercapnia, or carbon dioxide retention, is a listed hazard, but it is not a local nasal problem. Her problem is local to the nose, with bleeding and crusting. Tell: hypercapnia is retained carbon dioxide; mucosal irritation is local to the nose.

Correct. She has been on 6 L/min through a nasal cannula without humidification, and now has nosebleeds and a sore, crusted nose. Dry oxygen irritating the nasal lining is mucosal irritation, a listed hazard. Humidity is used when the flow is greater than 4 L/min.

Oxygen toxicity of the lungs is not among the listed hazards, which are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction. Her signs are in the nose, not the lungs. Tell: the listed hazard that affects the nose and airway lining is mucosal irritation.

E.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
E.q: A 72-year-old man with a long-term tracheostomy after head and neck cancer needs humidified supplemental oxygen at home. Which interface delivers air-entrainment nebulizer oxygen to his airway?
opts: Correct. He has a long-term tracheostomy and needs humidified oxygen delivered by an air-entrainment nebulizer. The trach collar is the air-entrainment nebulizer interface that fits over a tracheostomy, so it delivers to his airway directly.

A simple mask is a low flow device that covers the nose and mouth. It is not an air-entrainment nebulizer interface, and it would sit over a stoma he breathes through. Tell: the simple mask is a face interface with a variable fraction; the trach collar is the airway interface on this system.
ruled out by a stated finding

A nasal cannula sits in the nostrils, which would not reach a patient breathing through a tracheostomy, and it is a low flow device, not an air-entrainment one. Tell: the cannula is a nose device; the trach collar is the tracheostomy device.
ruled out by a stated finding

An open face mask is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface, but it sits over the face, as does the aerosol mask. A man who breathes through a tracheostomy needs the interface that fits the stoma. Tell: face interfaces are the aerosol and open face masks; the stoma interface is the trach collar.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 37-year-old man has acute bronchitis and is not given an antibiotic. He asks what to expect from his illness. Which counseling statement is accurate?
opts: The cough often lasts 2 to 3 weeks

Correct. Acute bronchitis is usually a self-limited viral infection, and the cough commonly lasts 2 to 3 weeks and may persist longer. Setting that expectation, and explaining that antibiotics do not significantly shorten the illness, is how unneeded antibiotic requests are reduced.
The cough should clear in 3 days

Three days badly underestimates the course; the cough commonly lasts 2 to 3 weeks and may persist longer. Promising 3 days invites a return visit and an antibiotic request while the cough is still there. Tell: a bronchitis cough is measured in weeks.
An antibiotic would halve the cough

Antibiotics do not significantly shorten the illness, and they bring adverse effects and resistance; many patients would need treatment to prevent one case of pneumonia. Tell: the evidence says antibiotics do not shorten this cough.
Green sputum means it is bacterial

Green or yellow mucus does not differentiate viral from bacterial infection, and colored sputum does not justify antibiotics. Tell: sputum color is not a marker of bacteria, so it is not a reason to return for an antibiotic.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
E.q: Which lung exam finding reflects a flattened diaphragm in this disease?
opts: Loud heart sounds at the apex
Heart sounds are distant and may be heard best at the epigastrium, not loud at the apex. Tell: the flattened-diaphragm sign is paradoxical lower intercostal retraction.
Neck veins that distend on inspiration
Jugular veins in this disease distend particularly during expiration. Tell: the flat-diaphragm sign is in the chest wall, with lower intercostal retraction on inspiration.

Correct. Paradoxical retraction of the lower intercostal spaces during inspiration reflects a flat diaphragm from hyperinflation. Other lung findings include decreased breath sounds in some areas with wheezing or crackles.
Hyperresonance in emphysema is generalized from hyperinflation, not limited to one apex. Tell: the sign linked to the flat diaphragm is the lower intercostal spaces pulling in during inspiration.

E.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
E.q: A 24-year-old woman has spirometry for suspected asthma. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is reduced with a reduced ratio, and it improves 14% after albuterol. How should this response be read?
opts: The threshold for a positive response is a 12% improvement, and her 14% rise is above it. Tell: compare the change with 12%; anything at or above it counts as a positive response.

Correct. Improvement of 12% or more in the forced expiratory volume in 1 second after a bronchodilator is a positive response, and her 14% rise meets it. A positive response on top of reduced baseline values strongly supports the diagnosis of asthma.
A 14% improvement after albuterol is reversal, the opposite of fixed obstruction. Tell: fixed obstruction would change little, while a rise above 12% marks reversible airflow limitation.
As a reason to skip spirometry next time
Spirometry is repeated annually to monitor progression, so a clear result now does not end its use. Tell: her 14% rise is a positive bronchodilator response, and spirometry stays part of follow-up.

E.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
E.q: A 47-year-old woman with a normal-gap metabolic acidosis has a bicarbonate of 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). By the Winter formula, what carbon dioxide range is expected with appropriate compensation?
opts: 24 to 28 uses 1.0 instead of 1.5 times bicarbonate (18 + 8 = 26). Winter uses 1.5: 35, so 33 to 37. Tell: multiply by one and a half.
25 to 29 is 1.5 x 18 = 27, plus or minus 2, without adding 8. Winter adds 8: 35, so 33 to 37. Tell: the formula is 1.5 times bicarbonate plus 8.

Correct. Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 18 + 8 = 27 + 8 = 35, plus or minus 2, so 33 to 37 mm Hg. A value above 37 would add a respiratory acidosis; below 33, a respiratory alkalosis.
36 to 44 is the normal carbon dioxide range. In metabolic acidosis the lungs lower carbon dioxide; Winter gives 33 to 37. Tell: a normal value here is under-compensation.

E.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
E.q: A 57-year-old smoker has chronic cough and mild breathlessness. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity of 0.76. How should this result be read?
opts: Asthma is supported by reversibility, 12% or more after a bronchodilator, not by a ratio above 0.70. Tell: this result simply fails to confirm obstruction.
It does not confirm the disease

Correct. The diagnosis requires a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70, and his is 0.76. Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, though smoking cessation remains essential for him.

A ratio of 0.76 is above the 0.70 cutoff, so obstruction is not confirmed. Tell: the diagnosis needs a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70. His cough may still be chronic bronchitis without obstruction.
Grades 1 to 4 are given only to patients whose ratio is below 0.70. Tell: without confirmed obstruction there is no grade to assign. Grade 2 also needs a 1-second volume of 50% to 79% predicted.

E.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
E.q: A 62-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease says she walks slower than friends her age on level ground because of breathlessness, but she does not need to stop. Which modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade fits?
opts: Grade 0 is breathlessness only with strenuous exercise. Tell: she is slowed on ordinary level walking, which is beyond grade 0. Grade 0 counts as fewer symptoms; she has more.
Grade 1 is shortness of breath when hurrying on the level or walking up a slight hill. Tell: she is slowed at a normal pace, not only when hurrying, which is grade 2.

Correct. Grade 2 is walking slower than people of the same age on the level because of breathlessness, or having to stop for breath at one's own pace on the level. A grade of 2 or more counts as more symptoms.
Grade 3 is stopping for breath after about 100 meters or a few minutes on the level. Tell: she does not need to stop, so she has not reached grade 3. Grade 2 already counts as more symptoms.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 33-year-old man has latent tuberculosis infection after household exposure to his brother, who has pulmonary tuberculosis; disease has been excluded in him. Besides possible drug interactions, what must be checked before a latent-infection regimen is chosen?
opts: A repeat skin test in 8 weeks

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for an early negative result in a contact; he already has latent infection. Tell: the check before choosing a regimen is source-case resistance.
A blood assay to confirm the skin test
A positive result already led to evaluation for disease, which was excluded; a second infection test does not guide the regimen. Tell: the factor to check is the source case's resistance.

Sputum cultures are followed until conversion during treatment of tuberculosis disease, which has been excluded in him. Tell: for latent infection the check before a regimen is source-case resistance.

Correct. Before a latent-infection regimen is chosen, interactions, pregnancy considerations and source-case resistance are checked, after disease has been excluded. His brother is the source case, so the brother's resistance pattern shapes which of the short regimens fits.

E.q: A 24-year-old woman with asthma has had fever, myalgias, cough and a sore throat for 30 hours, and influenza is confirmed by molecular testing. She is well enough for outpatient care. Which antiviral should be avoided?
opts: Intravenous peramivir is an option for eligible outpatients with uncomplicated influenza, with renal dose adjustment. Her asthma is irrelevant to an intravenous drug. Tell: bronchospasm risk belongs to the inhaled route.

Oseltamivir is the preferred influenza antiviral, including for high-risk patients, and asthma is no reason to avoid it. Tell: the antiviral with a breathing-specific warning is the inhaled one, zanamivir, because of bronchospasm.

Single-dose baloxavir is an option for uncomplicated influenza within 48 hours in eligible patients aged 5 or older; she is 24, at 30 hours, and not pregnant. Tell: asthma restricts the inhaled antiviral, not baloxavir.

Correct. Inhaled zanamivir is avoided in asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease because of the risk of bronchospasm. Her asthma makes it the antiviral to avoid; oseltamivir, single-dose baloxavir within 48 hours, or intravenous peramivir remain options for uncomplicated outpatient influenza.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. E.q: What is the preferred treatment for psittacosis in adults?
opts: Correct. Doxycycline is preferred in adults, started promptly when psittacosis is strongly suspected; improvement often begins within 48 to 72 hours. If tetracyclines are unsuitable, a macrolide is discussed with infectious disease, though macrolide failures have occurred.
Amoxicillin is a beta-lactam for healthy outpatients with typical community-acquired pneumonia. Tell: Chlamydia psittaci is an obligate intracellular bacterium, treated with doxycycline.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Tell: psittacosis is treated with doxycycline.
A macrolide is the alternative discussed with infectious disease when tetracyclines are unsuitable, and macrolide failures have occurred. Tell: the preferred adult drug is doxycycline.

E.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
E.q: A 72-year-old man has a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.48 and a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 26% predicted. Which airflow grade fits?
opts: Grade 1, mild, needs 80% predicted or more. At 26% he is far below. Tell: his airflow is about a quarter of predicted. His very low ratio and 26% airflow both show advanced obstruction.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted. At 26% he is well under it. Tell: under 30% is the very severe band. Moderate means at least half of predicted airflow.
Grade 3, severe, is 30% to 49% predicted. At 26% he has dropped below its lower limit. Tell: below 30% is grade 4. Severe stops at 30%; anything lower is very severe.
Correct. With the ratio below 0.70, a post-bronchodilator 1-second volume of 26% predicted is below 30%, grade 4, very severe. Grade 3 covers 30% to 49%.

E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: Which term names a pathologic condition with excessively alkaline body fluids or tissues?
opts: Hypocapnia, a low carbon dioxide, can produce an alkalosis but is a gas value, not the definition of the condition. The pathologic condition of excessively alkaline fluids is alkalosis. Tell: -capnia refers to carbon dioxide only.

Alkalemia is the blood finding, a pH above 7.45, not the underlying condition. The stem asks for the pathologic condition of excessively alkaline fluids or tissues, which is alkalosis. Tell: '-emia' is the number in blood, '-osis' is the process.

Acidosis is the condition of excessively acidic body fluids or tissues, the reverse of what the stem describes. The alkaline condition is alkalosis. Tell: the stem says alkaline, so look for the term built on alkal-.

Correct. Alkalosis is the pathologic condition of excessively alkaline body fluids or tissues. The resulting blood finding, a pH above 7.45, is called alkalemia, so the condition and the finding have different names.

E.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 40-year-old man who drank methanol is obtunded. Arterial blood gas: pH 6.65 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 18 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 2 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Besides treating the poisoning, what does this pH warrant?
opts: Rebreathing would raise carbon dioxide and lower the pH further; it is a placebo for hyperventilation. His low carbon dioxide is life-saving compensation. Tell: never blunt the breathing that compensates a metabolic acidosis.
Treating the cause is the rule, but a pH below 6.7 is unsustainable and may warrant therapy to normalize it as well. His 6.65 is past that threshold. Tell: extreme pH values earn their own therapy.
Therapy to raise the serum pH

Correct. A pH below 6.7 is unsustainable: it may cause cardiac hypocontractility and irritability, seizures and cerebral edema, and may warrant therapy to normalize the serum pH along with treatment of the underlying cause. His pH is 6.65.
He is already hyperventilating to a carbon dioxide of 18, and compensation never returns the pH to normal. At 6.65 the pH is unsustainable. Tell: compensation cannot rescue a pH below 6.7.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 2-year-old boy lives with an uncle who was diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis 6 weeks ago. The boy now has fever and cough, and his chest radiograph shows hilar adenopathy. Which stage of tuberculosis best fits?
opts: Correct. Progressive primary tuberculosis is disease that develops soon after initial infection when immune containment fails. Infancy and young childhood raise progression risk, his exposure is recent, and primary disease may show hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, infiltrates or effusion.
A primary infection may remain contained without clinical disease. Tell: containment has failed in this boy, because he has fever, cough and hilar adenopathy on his radiograph.

Latent infection is asymptomatic, with no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation and usually a normal chest radiograph. Tell: fever, cough and hilar adenopathy are disease, so he is beyond the latent stage.

Reactivation is latent infection that progresses to disease later, often with impaired immunity, after a period of containment. Tell: his disease followed a new exposure within weeks, the pattern of progressive primary disease.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
E.q: A 60-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and few symptoms asks to be started on an inhaled corticosteroid by itself because a friend with asthma uses one. Which regimen should be avoided in him?
opts: A single bronchodilator is the appropriate start for group A, few symptoms and low risk. Tell: it suits him; the regimen to avoid is a steroid inhaler used by itself.

Correct. In this disease, inhaled corticosteroids must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist, and then with a long-acting antimuscarinic as triple therapy, and cannot be used on their own. They also raise pneumonia risk. Alone, they are an asthma treatment.
Every patient should get the yearly influenza vaccine, which reduces hospitalizations and death. Tell: vaccination fits him; an inhaled corticosteroid alone is the regimen to avoid.
Smoking cessation is essential for every group and carries a survival benefit. Tell: it belongs in his plan; the steroid alone does not.

E.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
E.q: A 39-year-old man with asthma took aspirin at noon for a headache and developed facial flushing, a runny nose and wheezing at about 10 that night. He asks whether the aspirin could be responsible so many hours later. Which reply is accurate?
opts: No, aspirin sensitivity causes rash alone
Aspirin-sensitive asthma causes rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, facial flushing and wheezing, not a rash alone. Tell: his runny nose, flushing and wheeze match the listed reaction exactly.
Yes, but just selective agents cause it

The cross-reacting drugs are the non-selective anti-inflammatory agents, while selective ones such as celecoxib may be used. Tell: aspirin itself caused this reaction, which can be delayed up to 12 hours.

Reactions can occur within minutes but may also be delayed up to 12 hours, so a 10-hour gap does not rule out aspirin. Tell: the window extends to 12 hours, and his flushing, rhinorrhea and wheeze are the typical features.
Yes, reactions can be delayed up to 12 hours

Correct. In aspirin-sensitive asthma, symptoms may occur within minutes of aspirin ingestion or may be delayed up to 12 hours, and they include rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, facial flushing and wheezing. His reaction 10 hours after the dose fits.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
E.q: Which three conditions form the atopic triad?
opts: These are upper airway and eye problems, but the triad that defines atopy is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis. Tell: the triad spans three organs, nose, lungs and skin, and asthma is one of the three.

Food poisoning is an acute infection, not an allergic condition. The triad is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Tell: the triad members are allergic conditions; food poisoning is not.
Asthma, nasal polyps, and aspirin sensitivity

Nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity accompany intrinsic asthma, which is non-atopic with negative skin tests. The atopic triad is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis. Tell: a non-atopic cluster cannot be the atopic triad.
Allergic rhinitis, asthma, and atopic dermatitis

Correct. The atopic triad is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Finding one prompts questions about the others, and in extrinsic asthma the exam may show swollen nasal mucosa, increased secretions or eczema even when the chest is clear.

E.q: Which drugs make up the last 9 weeks of the 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen?
opts: Correct. The 17-week regimen gives isoniazid, rifapentine, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin for the first 8 weeks, then isoniazid, rifapentine and moxifloxacin for the next 9 weeks.
Rifampin with pyrazinamide belongs to the standard regimen's initial phase, not the rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen. Tell: the 17-week regimen keeps rifapentine and moxifloxacin throughout.
Ethambutol and rifampin belong to the standard 6-month regimen's start. Tell: the 17-week regimen ends on isoniazid, rifapentine and moxifloxacin.
Pyrazinamide stops after the first 8 weeks, and isoniazid continues. Tell: the last 9 weeks drop pyrazinamide and keep isoniazid, rifapentine and moxifloxacin.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
E.q: A 75-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is reviewed for comorbidities that become more important with age. Which condition should be added to his screening at this age?
opts: Correct. Comorbidities in older adults add osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline to cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease and depression. Inhaled corticosteroid-related fracture risk adds to the concern about bone health.
Exercise-induced bronchospasm is common in children and adolescents with asthma. Tell: older adults with this disease are screened for osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline.
Allergic rhinitis belongs to the atopic triad of asthma and is not on this disease's comorbidity list. Tell: the age-related additions are osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline.
Nasal polyps are common in intrinsic asthma, not an age-related comorbidity of this disease. Tell: screening at his age adds bone health and falls. They are not part of this disease's screening list.

E.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
E.q: A 44-year-old man who ingested ethylene glycol has an arterial pH of 6.62 (normal 7.35 to 7.45). Which complications does this pH threaten?
opts: Potassium entering cells is the shift of alkalosis. In acidosis potassium leaves cells, so hyperkalemia may be present. Tell: acidosis raises potassium.
Reduced release is an alkalosis effect (left shift). Acidosis lowers hemoglobin's affinity and increases release. Tell: the extreme-pH list is seizures, cerebral edema and cardiac effects.

Correct. A pH below 6.7 is unsustainable and may cause cardiac hypocontractility and irritability, seizures, cerebral edema and metabolic disturbances; it may warrant therapy to normalize the pH along with treating the cause.
Tetany from increased calcium binding with albumin occurs at a high pH, in severe respiratory alkalosis. His pH is 6.62. Tell: tetany belongs to alkalemia.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
E.q: A 25-year-old woman with allergic asthma triggered by cat dander is considering allergen immunotherapy against that single allergen. Which statement about this therapy applies to her?
opts: It works poorly against a single allergen
Immunotherapy is most useful in the context of single-allergen therapy, so her one identified trigger makes her a good candidate. Tell: single allergen is the favorable setting, not the poor one.
It can be self-given safely at home

Immunotherapy carries a risk of inducing bronchoconstriction that may need urgent treatment, so it is not self-given at home. Tell: the requirement is a controlled environment able to treat complications.
It must be given in a controlled setting

Correct. Immunotherapy may be considered when there are allergic triggers and is most useful against a single allergen, as for her cat dander. It must be done in a controlled environment because it can induce bronchoconstriction and may require urgent treatment of complications.
It is reserved for non-allergic asthma
Immunotherapy is considered for patients who have allergic triggers; non-allergic, intrinsic asthma lacks an allergen to target. Tell: her cat dander allergy is exactly the indication.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
E.q: A 72-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia is alert and oriented. Her blood urea nitrogen is 26 mg/dL, respiratory rate 24/min and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. What is her CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score?
opts: A total of 1 counts only one item, and she has two: urea above 20 mg/dL and age 65 or older. Tell: age scores a point by itself at 65 or older, so an older patient with any other item already has at least 2.

Correct. Confusion 0 (alert and oriented) + urea 1 (26 mg/dL is above 20) + respiratory rate 0 (24 is below 30) + blood pressure 0 (systolic not below 90, diastolic not 60 or lower) + age 1 (72) = 2. A total of 2 is moderate severity, with a risk of death of 9%, and the pathway sends her to the hospital.

A total of 3 adds a point she does not have: her respiratory rate of 24 is below 30, and her blood pressure of 128/76 is not low. Tell: only urea and age score here; 3 or more would be high severity, with a risk of death of 15 to 40%.

A total of 4 would need two more items, such as confusion and low blood pressure, and she is alert with a normal blood pressure. Tell: 4 or 5 is the band where transfer to critical care is especially considered, far above her two points.

E.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
E.q: Which delivery device is classed as a high flow device?
opts: A simple mask is a low flow device, set between 5 and 10 L/min, and its delivered fraction varies with the patient's breathing. The Venturi mask is the one classed as high flow. Tell: the simple mask is low flow.

Correct. The Venturi mask is classed as a high flow device, and it allows precise delivery of oxygen, with different ports changing the fraction delivered. The flow is adjusted from 4 to 10 L/min to give 24% to 50%.

A non-rebreather mask is described as a low flow device, but with high fraction, despite its 60% to 100% output. The Venturi mask is the one classed as high flow. Tell: a high fraction does not make it high flow.
A nasal cannula is a low flow device, set at 1 to 6 L/min. The high flow device among these choices is the Venturi mask. Tell: low flow versus high flow is the classification.

E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 36-year-old man is confused after drinking antifreeze (ethylene glycol). Sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L), chloride 102 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
opts: Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 140 - (102 + 8) = 140 - 110 = 30, above the normal 9 to 15: an elevated-gap metabolic acidosis, fitting ethylene glycol, the E of the mnemonic.

34 adds the potassium of 4.0 to the sodium. The formula used here is sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate), with no potassium: 140 - 110 = 30. Tell: potassium is not part of this anion gap formula.
38 is 140 - 102, leaving out the bicarbonate. Both measured anions are subtracted: 140 - (102 + 8) = 30. Tell: the gap subtracts chloride and bicarbonate.
46 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (140 - 102 + 8). The bicarbonate sits inside the parentheses with chloride: 140 - (102 + 8) = 30. Tell: check the sign of the bicarbonate.

Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: Recent hotel or cruise ship travel raises concern for which pneumonia pathogen?
opts: Blastomyces dermatitidis is linked with travel to or residence in southeastern and south-central states bordering the Mississippi and Ohio River basins. Tell: hotel or cruise ship exposure points to Legionella.

Correct. Hotel or cruise ship travel in the past two weeks is linked with Legionella species, which favors confined spaces and areas with circulating water droplets such as hot tubs or fountains. Legionella is one of the atypical pathogens.
Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) is linked with exposure to farm animals or parturient cats. Tell: travel on a cruise ship or stay in a hotel points to Legionella.
Histoplasma capsulatum comes from soil with bat or bird droppings, mainly in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. Tell: water droplets in hotels and cruise ships point to Legionella.

E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 29-year-old man hikes to 4,000 meters and develops headache and breathlessness. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.50 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 22 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Metabolic acidosis has a low pH, and his is 7.50. The low carbon dioxide of 29 is the primary change, not compensation. Tell: compensation never overcorrects, so the pH identifies the primary disorder.

Correct. The pH of 7.50 is alkalemia, and the carbon dioxide of 29 is low and matches it (respiratory). Bicarbonate fell about 2 per 10 mm Hg (11 below 40 gives about 22), the acute response. High altitude drives hypoxia-induced hyperventilation.
Metabolic alkalosis needs a high bicarbonate, and his is 22. The low carbon dioxide matches his alkalemia. Tell: a high pH with a low carbon dioxide is respiratory.
ruled out by a stated finding

Chronic compensation would lower bicarbonate about 5 per 10 mm Hg, to about 18 (11 below 40). His 22 shows only the acute response after a single climb. Tell: a short exposure gives the acute pattern.

E.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
E.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with allergic asthma asks whether keeping her baby away from dust, pets and pollen will prevent the child from developing asthma. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Avoidance matters just for pet dander
No single allergen is singled out; allergen avoidance in general does not reduce the risk of developing asthma. Tell: avoidance controls triggers in someone who has asthma, but does not prevent it.

Avoiding allergens does not reduce the risk of developing asthma, so strict avoidance is not prevention. Tell: early exposure may be protective through tolerance, the opposite of what strict avoidance assumes.
Early exposure may be protective through tolerance, and not all atopic individuals develop asthma. Tell: exposure early in life is not a cause the evidence supports avoiding.
Avoidance does not lower the risk

Correct. Inhaled allergens are common triggers and are implicated in sensitization, but avoiding allergens does not reduce the risk of developing asthma, and early exposure may even be protective by building tolerance.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 49-year-old woman on targeted testing for tuberculosis infection has an interferon-gamma release assay reported as indeterminate. She has no symptoms. Which next test is most appropriate?
opts: Repeat the assay or use a skin test

Correct. An indeterminate, invalid or borderline interferon-gamma release assay is handled by repeating the assay or using a tuberculin skin test as clinically appropriate. An indeterminate result says nothing either way about infection, so another immune-response test is needed.
An indeterminate result does not show infection, and even a positive one needs evaluation for disease before any treatment. Tell: repeat the assay or use a skin test first.
Sputum testing is for symptoms or suspicious imaging suggesting pulmonary disease. Tell: she is symptom-free, so the indeterminate blood test is simply repeated or replaced by a skin test.
Treat as negative; no further testing
Indeterminate is not negative: it is a nonresult that calls for repeating the assay or using a skin test. Tell: even a true negative leaves disease possible, and this result is not even negative.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 54-year-old woman who had a kidney transplant takes long-term prednisone and anti-rejection drugs. She has 10 days of progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough, and her chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Induced sputum microscopy and Pneumocystis molecular testing are negative, but suspicion remains high. Which test should be done next?
opts: Spontaneously expectorated sputum has poor sensitivity for Pneumocystis and should not be used to exclude the infection. After a negative induced sample, a weaker specimen adds nothing. Tell: the step after a negative induced sputum goes deeper, to lavage, not back to plain sputum.

Pulmonary function testing is not a routine acute diagnostic test for Pneumocystis, and a normal diffusing capacity cannot reliably exclude it. Tell: she needs organism confirmation from the lower airway, which lavage provides and a breathing test cannot.

Lactate dehydrogenase is nonspecific and cannot confirm Pneumocystis or establish treatment failure. Her problem is a negative specimen with high suspicion, which only a better respiratory sample can answer. Tell: a nonspecific blood marker cannot replace microbiologic confirmation.

Correct. A negative induced specimen does not exclude Pneumocystis, and bronchoalveolar lavage is considered when induced sputum is negative and suspicion remains high. Her transplant, steroid use and perihilar infiltrates keep suspicion high, and the lavage sample goes for microscopy or molecular testing and other infections.

E.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: Which chloride pattern goes with normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
opts: Chloride does change: in normal-gap acidosis it rises (hyperchloremic) to balance the lost bicarbonate. Tell: the key finding is a high chloride with a low bicarbonate.
Correct. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis is hyperchloremic, since chloride rises as bicarbonate falls. Elevated anion gap acidosis is normochloremic, because other anions replace the bicarbonate.

Normochloremia goes with the elevated-gap type, where unmeasured anions replace bicarbonate. The normal-gap type is hyperchloremic. Tell: normal chloride means unmeasured anions, high chloride means a normal gap.
Low chloride appears in metabolic alkalosis and chronic respiratory acidosis. Normal-gap acidosis is hyperchloremic. Tell: low chloride goes with alkalosis states.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 52

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
E.q: A 39-year-old man with asthma takes ibuprofen for a sprained ankle. Within 20 minutes he develops a runny nose, red irritated eyes, facial flushing and wheezing. Which diagnosis explains the reaction?
opts: Exercise-induced bronchospasm follows exertion, and a sprained ankle is not exercise. Tell: the reaction followed a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug and included flushing, rhinorrhea and eye irritation, the aspirin-sensitive picture.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. About 1 to 5% of asthmatics worsen with aspirin, and patients with true aspirin sensitivity cross-react with non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen. Rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, facial flushing and wheezing within minutes of the dose is the described reaction.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity to the Aspergillus mold, not to a drug. Tell: the timing after ibuprofen and the flushing and eye symptoms identify aspirin sensitivity with cross-reactivity to a non-selective agent.

Cardiac asthma is wheezing from decompensated heart failure, and he has no heart failure. Tell: wheeze with flushing, a runny nose and eye irritation minutes after ibuprofen is a drug reaction, not a cardiac cause.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
E.q: What is the most common reason for poor symptom control in refractory asthma?
opts: Correct. Refractory asthma takes two forms, persistent symptoms with poor lung function or normal function with severe exacerbations; non-compliance is the most common reason for poor symptom control, and steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon.
Steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon. Non-compliance is the most common reason for poor symptom control. Tell: before blaming the drug, check whether the patient is actually taking it correctly.

Aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity seen in asthma that causes exacerbations, but it is not the most common reason for poor control; non-compliance is. Tell: the commonest cause is behavioral, not a second disease.

Exercise-induced bronchospasm is predictable and prevented with pre-exercise and regular controller therapy. Non-compliance is the usual cause of poor control. Tell: exercise symptoms come and go with activity, while refractory asthma means poor control despite treatment.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 63-year-old man has a chest radiograph showing fibrotic upper-lobe scarring that suggests prior tuberculosis, and he has never been treated for it. His tuberculin skin test shows 6 mm of induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Correct. Imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis places him in the 5 mm group, together with human immunodeficiency virus, recent close contact, transplant and major immunosuppression. 6 mm meets that cut-off, and his fibrotic lesion also warrants review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease.
Negative; old scars cause false results

The listed causes of a false-positive skin test are bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination and some nontuberculous exposures; false negatives come from early infection, immunosuppression or severe disease. Tell: his scarring is a 5 mm risk group, not a source of error.
10 mm is for increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings and children under 5. Tell: scarring that suggests prior tuberculosis belongs to the 5 mm group.
15 mm applies when there are no known risk factors. Tell: a radiograph suggesting prior tuberculosis is itself a 5 mm risk, so his 6 mm is positive.

E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 26-year-old man is found unresponsive at a party with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.24 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 62 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate driving the low pH, and his bicarbonate is 26, within normal. The raised carbon dioxide of 62 is the value that matches the acidemia. Tell: when bicarbonate is normal and carbon dioxide is high, the problem is respiratory.
ruled out by a stated finding

Respiratory alkalosis is a high pH from a low carbon dioxide. He has a pH of 7.24 and a carbon dioxide of 62, and both point the other way. Tell: check the pH first; 7.24 is acidemia, so no alkalosis is possible.

Chronic respiratory acidosis would show a much larger bicarbonate rise, about 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg, or near 32 here (22 mm Hg above 40). His 26 is the small acute rise. Tell: a bicarbonate near 26 means the kidneys have not had their 6 to 12 hours or more.

Correct. The pH of 7.24 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 62 is high, which matches it, so the problem is respiratory. Bicarbonate rose only about 1 per 10 mm Hg (22 above 40 gives about 26), the acute response. A slow rate of 6 fits central nervous system depression.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

E.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
E.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic lung disease has been vomiting for days. His bicarbonate is 40 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), his pH 7.46 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), and his carbon dioxide 58 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). What does the carbon dioxide level indicate?
opts: His bicarbonate is 40 and his pH 7.46, both on the alkaline side, so there is no metabolic acidosis. The high carbon dioxide suggests an added respiratory acidosis. Tell: a metabolic acidosis would lower the bicarbonate.

Correct. In metabolic alkalosis, respiratory compensation rarely raises carbon dioxide above 55 mm Hg. His 58 is above that (and above 52, the 16 x 0.75 rise from 40), so a concurrent primary respiratory acidosis fits, along with his chronic lung disease.

Compensation for metabolic alkalosis rarely takes carbon dioxide above 55, and his 58 is past that limit, so compensation alone does not explain it. Tell: the 55 ceiling separates compensation from a second disorder.
ruled out by a stated finding

A respiratory alkalosis would lower carbon dioxide, and his is 58, which is high. The excess points to a concurrent respiratory acidosis. Tell: respiratory alkalosis would pull carbon dioxide below normal.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

E.io: Explain the rationale for a nebulizer treatment.
E.q: A 52-year-old woman with chronic lung disease has thick secretions she struggles to cough up during a severe exacerbation. Besides medication delivery, which listed rationale for a nebulizer applies?
opts: Correct. Her thick secretions that she cannot cough up in a severe exacerbation match secretion clearance, which is a listed rationale for a nebulizer along with delivering liquid medication directly to the airways. The nebulizer helps move the mucus.

A nebulizer delivers liquid medication to the airways and does not replace oxygen. If she needs oxygen she still requires an oxygen delivery device. Tell: a nebulizer carries medication and helps clear secretions; oxygen delivery is a separate need.

Delivering a fixed oxygen fraction is a feature of air-entrainment devices such as the Venturi mask, which hold the fraction steady regardless of demand. It is not the stated reason for a nebulizer, and it does not address her secretions. Tell: the fixed fraction is about oxygen; her problem is mucus.

Preventing carbon dioxide retention is not a listed rationale for a nebulizer. Carbon dioxide retention is a hazard of oxygen therapy, and her stem describes a mucus problem. Tell: the nebulizer is for medication and secretion clearance, not for guarding against hypercapnia.

E.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
E.q: A 26-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant comes in during October and asks about vaccines. Which vaccine should be avoided during her pregnancy?
opts: An age-appropriate recombinant vaccine may be used in any trimester of pregnancy. Tell: inactivated and recombinant vaccines are both acceptable; the live attenuated vaccine is the one avoided.
Tdap is given during every pregnancy to protect against pertussis. Tell: Tdap is one of the vaccines recommended in pregnancy, so it is not the one to avoid.
An age-appropriate inactivated vaccine is recommended in any trimester of pregnancy. Tell: the restriction in pregnancy is on the live attenuated product, not on inactivated vaccine.

Correct. In pregnancy, influenza vaccination uses an age-appropriate inactivated or recombinant vaccine in any trimester, and the live attenuated vaccine is avoided. Live attenuated vaccine has pregnancy and immunocompromise restrictions, so her pregnancy rules it out.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
E.q: A 67-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a resting oxygen saturation of 91% on room air, and she stays at 91% during a walking test. She asks for home oxygen. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Correct. A resting saturation of 89% to 93% is moderate resting desaturation, with no indication for long-term oxygen, and her saturation stays at 91% with exertion. Oxygen is indicated with severe hypoxemia, an arterial oxygen pressure under 55 mmHg or saturation of 88% or less.
She needs oxygen over 15 hours a day
Long-term oxygen for more than 15 hours a day requires severe resting desaturation, 88% or less. Tell: her 91% is moderate desaturation, which does not qualify.
She needs a sleep study first
A sleep apnea evaluation is for desaturation at night only. Tell: her daytime readings are moderate, and nothing suggests nocturnal-only desaturation.
Exertional oxygen is for desaturation to 88% or less with exertion. She stays at 91% while walking. Tell: moderate exertional desaturation, 89% to 93%, gives no indication.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
E.q: A 33-year-old man with asthma has symptoms 1 day a week, wakes at night once a month, uses albuterol 1 day a week, and has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 91% predicted. In the past year, however, he needed 3 separate courses of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations. How should his asthma be classified?
opts: His day-to-day impairment alone fits intermittent asthma, but the risk domain counts too, and intermittent allows only 0 to 1 steroid-requiring exacerbation a year. He had 3. Tell: the risk domain can move a quiet patient into persistent asthma.

Correct. His impairment is intermittent-level, but patients with 2 or more exacerbations requiring oral systemic corticosteroids in the past year may be considered the same as patients with persistent asthma, even without persistent-level impairment. Three steroid courses put him in the persistent risk row.

Three steroid-requiring exacerbations in a year are not well controlled; the risk domain treats 2 or more as persistent asthma. Tell: a good week-to-week picture does not cancel repeated exacerbations.

Nothing ties his symptoms to exercise, and exercise-induced bronchospasm does not explain repeated steroid-requiring exacerbations. Tell: the decisive fact is the count of oral steroid courses, 3 in a year, which defines persistent risk.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
E.q: A 15-year-old soccer player develops cough and wheezing within minutes of hard running, peaking about 10 minutes later and resolving within an hour. She is otherwise symptom-free. Which treatment should she use before exercise?
opts: A long-acting beta-2 agonist has no anti-inflammatory effect and should not be used as monotherapy in asthma. Tell: the pre-exercise treatment for exercise-induced bronchospasm is the short-acting agent.

Tiotropium is an anticholinergic with a slow onset of action and is less effective than beta-2 agonists, so it suits neither quick protection nor her pattern. Tell: a short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise is the treatment for exercise-induced bronchospasm.

Short systemic corticosteroid courses control exacerbations; she has brief, predictable symptoms only with exercise. Tell: exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise and best prevented with a regular inhaled steroid.

Correct. Her symptoms begin within minutes of exercise, peak at 10 to 15 minutes and resolve by an hour, the exercise-induced bronchospasm pattern. An inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist used before exercise decreases the bronchoconstriction.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: Which is the most sensitive routine diagnostic test for coronavirus disease 2019?
opts: Correct. Nucleic acid amplification, including polymerase chain reaction, is the most sensitive routine diagnostic method, using an assay-validated specimen. One negative antigen test does not exclude infection.
Chest imaging evaluates pneumonia and complications, not the viral cause by itself. Tell: the virus is diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification.
D-dimer elevation alone does not diagnose thrombosis or set anticoagulant intensity, and it does not diagnose the infection. Tell: use nucleic acid amplification.
One negative antigen test does not exclude infection; repeat testing after 48 hours or nucleic acid amplification is needed. Tell: amplification is the most sensitive routine test.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 54-year-old woman vomits and aspirates during a witnessed seizure. Two hours later she has abrupt shortness of breath and hypoxemia, a temperature of 100.6°F and a white blood cell count of 13,500/µL. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Anaerobic coverage is added when an abscess or empyema is suspected, not routinely after aspiration, and she has a sterile chemical injury. Tell: anaerobic coverage is reserved for abscess or empyema.

Ampicillin-sulbactam is the usual first choice for lung abscess, and antibiotics are not given prophylactically after aspiration when bacterial infection is not suspected. Tell: chemical injury needs support; established infection needs antibiotics.

A community-acquired pneumonia regimen treats aspiration pneumonia, an established infection with a compatible infiltrate, not a sterile chemical injury 2 hours after a witnessed event. Tell: her fever and white count can occur without any infection.

Correct. A witnessed aspiration of gastric contents followed within hours by abrupt respiratory decline is aspiration pneumonitis, a sterile chemical injury; fever or leukocytosis can occur without bacterial infection. Support oxygenation and the airway, and avoid prophylactic antibiotics when bacterial infection is not suspected.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 2-year-old girl lives with her grandmother, who was just diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. The girl is well, and her first tuberculin skin test shows 0 mm of induration. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: When repeat testing is indicated after a recent exposure, it is done 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure, not a year later. Tell: a young child contact cannot wait; she needs prompt public-health assessment now.

The 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen treats drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis disease in patients aged 12 or older. Tell: she is 2 years old and well, with no disease found, so a disease regimen is the wrong tool.

Correct. Early infection can produce a negative skin test, so one negative result soon after exposure does not settle it. Young children and immunocompromised contacts need prompt public-health assessment, and infancy and young childhood carry a higher risk of progression after infection.

Early infection can produce a negative tuberculin skin test, so a result taken soon after exposure cannot clear her. Tell: she is a young child exposed at home, a contact group singled out for prompt public-health assessment.
